author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Self-duality forces p_c + p_c^* = 1 only when the crossing probabilities at the self-dual point are bounded away from 0 and 1; without a box-crossing property the fixed point of the duality map need not be critical.
method: Ask what a nonvacuous version of the question could say, by cataloguing the only two mechanisms that have ever produced an exact p_c: (i) a self-duality that forces the critical point to a fixed point of the duality map, upgraded to an identification by a box-crossing (RSW) property; (ii) an exact recursion on a tree or a tree-like transitive graph.
obstruction: No invariant of a transitive graph is known that predicts whether p_c is algebraic. Every existing proof of an exact value runs through an algebraic identity between the model and its dual, and no such identity exists off the star-triangle family, so one cannot even rule out that p_c of some simple non-self-dual planar lattice is transcendental. The density reformulation is not free either: it needs a family along which p_c moves continuously, and continuity of p_c is known only along the slab approximations of Grimmett-Marstrand.
result: Mechanism (i) is not a property of the graph alone but of a pair (graph, dual): it delivers p_c only when the duality map has a unique fixed point in (0,1) AND the crossing probabilities at that point are bounded away from 0 and 1. That is why the star-triangle family (square, triangular, hexagonal, and the isoradial graphs of Grimmett-Manolescu) is the natural closure of the method, and why it stops there. Mechanism (ii) gives p_c = 1/(b-1) on the b-ary tree and survives on nonamenable Cayley graphs only in the qualitative form p_c < 1, not as a formula. A version of the question with content, which the known values can already address, is: is the set {p_c(G) : G an infinite connected vertex-transitive graph} dense in (0,1)? The known values accumulate at 0 (p_c(Z^d) is asymptotically 1/(2d)) and at 1 (long-range one-dimensional chains), so density is the natural sharpening rather than a search for more closed forms. This is a reformulation of the source's question, not progress on it.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: P_p{|C| >= n} = sum over m >= n of P_p{|C| = m} with a nondecreasing exponent in m; the two rates agree exactly when the sum is dominated by its first term, so the whole content is that the exponent is not flat to leading order over a window of length n.
method: Split the question into the half the Wulff theory delivers and the half it does not. Write W_p for the Wulff constant, the infimum of the integral of the surface tension over the boundary of a body of unit volume, so that the surface-order LDP for the monotone event reads -lim n^{-(d-1)/d} log P_p{|C(v)| >= n} = W_p.
obstruction: Trimming a supercritical cluster is not local: closing boundary sites to shed volume can disconnect the droplet, or merge the finite cluster with the infinite one and destroy the conditioning event {|C(v)| < infinity}. Any repair must control the volume through an event measurable with respect to Pisztora's coarse-grained block field, and that field resolves volumes only up to a multiplicative factor (1 + eps) - precisely the resolution an exact-volume question refuses.
result: The upper half is immediate: {|C(v)| = n} is contained in {|C(v)| >= n}, so limsup n^{-(d-1)/d} log P_p{|C(v)| = n} <= -W_p, given only the monotone LDP. The matching lower bound is a volume-adjustment statement: it would suffice to modify a near-Wulff cluster of volume in [n, n + n^{(d-1)/d}] into one of volume exactly n at cost exp(o(n^{(d-1)/d})). Here is the budget that decides the problem, and it is the reason the naive argument fails: adding or deleting m boundary sites costs at most exp(Cm), while the surplus volume to be shed is itself of order n^{(d-1)/d} - exactly the order of the entire exponent. The trimming argument is therefore critical, not subcritical. Stating where the two rates could differ is sharper than the source's own remark, but it is a localisation of the difficulty, not a proof that the limit exists.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: theta = inf_n P_p(v <-> partial B_n): an infimum of continuous increasing functions is upper semicontinuous, which gives right continuity for free and leaves only the left limit in question.
method: Separate the two statements the question conflates: continuity in the interior of the interval, and the boundary value at p_c.
obstruction: A jump of theta at some p in (p_c, p_u) would mean a positive density of vertices joins the infinite clusters at a single parameter. Excluding it by a Russo derivative bound needs an influence estimate at p, and in the non-uniqueness phase the pivotal vertex for {v lies in an infinite cluster} need not be unique or locally identifiable, since v may join any of infinitely many infinite clusters. The mass-transport principle controls the NUMBER of infinite clusters but says nothing about theta itself.
result: Right continuity is free everywhere and needs no hypothesis: theta(p) = inf_n P_p(v <-> boundary of B_n) is a decreasing limit of polynomials in p, hence upper semicontinuous, and theta is nondecreasing, so theta is right continuous on [0,1]. Left continuity on any interval where the infinite cluster is a.s. unique is the van den Berg-Keane argument. The live content of the question is therefore exactly the non-uniqueness window (p_c, p_u), where the infinite cluster has infinitely many components and the van den Berg-Keane proof, which uses uniqueness to prevent the number of infinite clusters from jumping, is simply unavailable. Saying it this way is sharper than the source's reduction, which only records the p_c = p_u case. What is NOT claimed: nothing here suggests left continuity fails on (p_c, p_u); the honest status of the interior is 'no known proof', not 'expected to fail'.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Aizenman-Barsky and Aizenman-Newman give the mean-field bounds beta <= 1, gamma >= 1, delta >= 2 with no exponent existence assumed; existence is a separate, unaddressed statement.
method: Ask which of the three demands is logically weakest, since the source poses them as one problem; order them existence, scaling relations, universality, and test whether that order is right.
obstruction: Existence of an exponent asserts that a log-log slope has a genuine limit, and percolation offers no subadditivity in p to force one. The only tool that produces exponents, the lace expansion, needs the triangle condition, a strictly high-dimensional input false in d = 3, 4, 5; the two-dimensional tools (RSW, conformal invariance) are planar. Dimensions three to five have neither, and that is the entire difficulty.
result: The order is wrong in one place, and that is the useful observation: scaling relations are NOT downstream of existence. Several are proved as two-sided inequalities between limsup and liminf exponents by differential-inequality arguments (Aizenman-Barsky, Aizenman-Newman) that never assume a limit exists. So the honest decomposition is that the relations already hold in inequality form and what is missing is the coincidence of limsup and liminf. Universality is strictly harder than both and has no route that avoids an exactly solved representative of the class - which is why even the two-dimensional case, where only site percolation on the triangular lattice is solved, is not a proof of universality. A caution about what does not count as progress: if the exponents exist, Fisher's relation gamma = nu(2 - eta) follows from the definitions plus the infrared bound and carries no extra information.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: theta(p) <= P_{p_c}(0 <-> partial B_{L(p)}): the missing power bound on theta is exactly a missing polynomial critical one-arm bound together with a power relation for the near-critical correlation length.
method: Test how much of the missing bound is already forced by the inequalities the source itself quotes, in particular Kesten's chi(p) >= C |log(p_c - p)|^{-(d-1)/d} (p_c - p)^{-1/d} for p < p_c, obtained by iterating the critical crossing estimate over k blocks.
obstruction: Every known proof of an upper bound on theta near criticality goes through the one-arm probability at p_c, via theta(p) <= P_{p_c}(0 <-> partial B_{L(p)}) with L(p) the near-critical correlation length, and then needs polynomial decay of the critical one-arm probability. That decay comes from RSW in d = 2 and from the lace expansion in high dimensions. In d = 3, 4, 5 there is no proof that P_{p_c}(0 <-> partial B_n) decays polynomially at all, and without it no power of |p - p_c| can be produced by any known relation for L(p).
result: That chain gives a power lower bound on chi with a poor exponent and gives nothing at all on theta, because the passage from chi to theta needs the other direction. The point that must be stated carefully: Aizenman-Barsky's inequality theta(p) >= c(p - p_c) is a LOWER bound on theta, and the mean-field bound beta <= 1 is a statement in the same direction; neither supplies the sought upper bound theta(p) <= C(p - p_c)^{C'}, and no trivial inequality does. What the reduction does give is an equivalence worth recording: an upper bound of that form is exactly a quantitative version of continuity of theta at p_c, which is the statement missing in d = 3, 4, 5.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: N(v) is a sum over dyadic scales of per-annulus closed-vertex costs; in d = 2 both the log|v| mean and the log|v| variance follow from tightness plus asymptotic independence of those costs, so one tightness statement decides the shape of the answer in every dimension.
method: Ask what the two-dimensional proof actually uses and which ingredient survives in d >= 3. The Z^2 argument renormalises over dyadic annuli: at each of the log|v| scales the path must cross a critical annulus, the closed-vertex cost per annulus is tight, the costs are asymptotically independent across scales by RSW decoupling, and the CLT is a Lindeberg sum over scales.
obstruction: Cross-scale decoupling in d = 2 is RSW. There is no RSW in d >= 3, and the only decoupling available for critical percolation there is the high-dimensional two-point function estimate, a statement about connection probabilities rather than about the number of closed vertices on an optimal path. Worse, in d >= 3 an optimal path has more ways to route around obstacles, so the per-scale cost is plausibly growing rather than tight, and the trivial |v|^{eps} bound does not even exclude a polynomial mean.
result: Both the mean of order log|v| and the standard deviation of order (log|v|)^{1/2} come from the same structure - one asymptotically independent O(1) contribution per scale. Consequently the shape of the answer in d >= 3 is decided by a single question: is the per-scale cost still tight? If it is, the same Lindeberg argument gives E N(v) asymptotically c log|v| and a central limit theorem with variance of order log|v|, in any dimension where a cross-scale decoupling is available. This collapses the source's two demands ('improve the bound' and 'find a limit theorem') into one estimate. It is a reduction, not a bound: tightness of the per-scale cost is precisely what is unknown.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The mean-field one-type equilibrium is 1 - delta_i/beta_i, so beta_1/delta_1 > beta_2/delta_2 is exactly the statement that type 1 has the larger mean-field carrying capacity; the spatial claim is that a single lattice preserves that ordering.
method: Locate the exact place where the equal-death-rate proof breaks. Neuhauser's argument for equal delta uses the multitype duality: the two types share one graphical construction, and the ancestral process of a site is a single coalescing branching random walk whose type is decided by the initial condition it reaches, so the competition is settled by a single comparison of birth rates.
obstruction: The two-type system with unequal death rates is not attractive in the coordinatewise order that makes type 1 grow at the expense of type 2 (increasing type 1 both helps type 1 and, by occupying sites, hurts type 2 - the standard order works only when the death rates agree so that vacancies are exchangeable). Without attractiveness there is no monotone coupling, without duality there is no ancestral computation, and the block construction gives coexistence results but not exclusion results, because exclusion is an upper bound on one type and the block construction only produces lower bounds.
result: With delta_1 different from delta_2 that duality is destroyed, and not for a technical reason: a type-i particle dies at rate delta_i, so the ancestral lineage of a site would have to know its own type in order to run its death clock. The dual is therefore a TYPE-DEPENDENT branching-coalescing walk, and the type is exactly what one is trying to determine - the duality is circular. The quantity beta_i/delta_i is the mean-field invasion fitness (the mean-field equilibrium density of type i alone is 1 - delta_i/beta_i, increasing in beta_i/delta_i), so the conjecture says the spatial model respects the mean-field ordering. That is not automatic: the spatial critical value of the one-type contact process is beta/delta > lambda_c > 1, so the spatial fitness ordering could in principle differ from the mean-field one; what saves the conjecture, if it is true, is that both types feel the SAME lattice, so the map (beta, delta) -> spatial invasion speed should be monotone in beta/delta by a scaling of time. This scaling observation is the natural first step and it is not in the source; it does not prove the conjecture because time scaling does not act on the two types simultaneously.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For convex phi and a probability kernel J, Jensen gives phi(J*u) <= J*phi(u); hence the fast-stirring Lyapunov inequality dh/dt <= Laplacian h + phi'(u).f(u) becomes dh/dt <= J*h - h + phi'(u).f(u) with no extra hypothesis.
method: Carry the proof of Theorem 5 through with the diffusive limit replaced by the nonlocal limit. Under long-range interaction of range N, the hydrodynamic object is not u_t = Laplacian u + f(u) but the nonlocal equation u_t = J*u - u + f(u), where J is the normalised interaction kernel.
obstruction: The spreading step is where long range and fast stirring genuinely differ. For the diffusive equation, 'one pile makes two piles' follows from a finite-speed travelling front. For the nonlocal equation the front speed is finite only when J has exponential tails; for heavy-tailed J the fronts accelerate and the block construction's fixed space-time box has no analogue. Moreover the long-range particle system does not converge to the nonlocal PDE with a small parameter multiplying the noise the way fast stirring does: as the range N grows the fluctuation term is of order N^{-d/2} and the error in the hydrodynamic approximation must be beaten uniformly over the block, which is exactly what the case-by-case proofs do by hand.
result: The Lyapunov step survives, and the hypothesis that survives it is exactly the one the source already assumes. Set h = phi(u) with phi convex. Jensen's inequality applied to the probability kernel J gives phi(J*u) <= J*phi(u), i.e. phi(J*u) - phi(u) <= (J*h - h). Combining with dphi/dt along the ODE, the same computation that produced dh/dt <= Laplacian h + phi'(u).f(u) in the diffusive case yields dh/dt <= J*h - h + phi'(u).f(u) in the nonlocal case, and the right-hand side is again 'nonlocal heat flow with killing' since phi'(u).f(u) <= 0 by hypothesis (i). So convexity of phi, which in the fast-stirring proof was used against the Laplacian, is precisely the hypothesis that makes the nonlocal generator work, and no new hypothesis on phi is needed. What this does NOT do: it gives the differential inequality, not the coexistence theorem, because the block construction still needs a spreading statement for the nonlocal equation.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: No interior mean-field fixed point does not imply no spatial coexistence: the catalyst model in the same survey coexists in a parameter range that the source's own mean-field analysis does not predict.
method: Ask what kind of statement 'no coexistence' is, and which of the two standard machines can produce it. Coexistence is a lower bound on both densities and is produced by the block construction; non-coexistence is an upper bound on one density and is produced either by a monotone coupling with a subcritical process or by a Lyapunov/entropy argument on the whole configuration.
obstruction: The comparison requires a monotone coupling of a three-type system, and three-type contact processes are not attractive in any order that keeps both comparisons simultaneously: making the 3s more numerous helps the 3s and hurts the 2s, but it also changes the environment the 1s see, and there is no partial order on {1,2,3} that is preserved by the dynamics. The absence of an interior fixed point is a mean-field fact and does not survive the spatial fluctuation, so the mean-field computation is a heuristic and not an ingredient of a proof.
result: The absence of an interior fixed point in the mean-field ODE, which the source records, is not by itself an obstruction to spatial coexistence, and it is important not to read it as one: spatial models routinely coexist where the ODE does not (the catalyst example in the same survey, and cyclic systems, are exactly of that kind). So the mean-field computation cannot be the proof. The route that has content is the invasion argument the source sketches, made into a comparison: if the 3s invade a 1-2 equilibrium and their advantage is monotone increasing in their own density, the density of 3s dominates a supercritical growth process and the 2s are dominated by a subcritical one. The needed structure is monotonicity of the 2s' effective death rate in the density of 3s, which holds exactly in the mutualist ordering lambda_2 < lambda_3 < lambda_1 - and that is the reason the ordering appears in the conjecture.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Two-sided block bounds pin the density of every nontrivial stationary law to an interval shrinking with eps, but equality of densities is not equality of laws - the missing ingredient is a coupling, not a better estimate.
method: Ask what a uniqueness proof would have to supply beyond what the block construction already gives, by pushing the block construction as far as it goes.
obstruction: Uniqueness for interacting particle systems is proved either by attractiveness plus a complete convergence theorem, or by duality. The sexual reproduction model is not attractive (birth requires TWO occupied neighbours, so adding particles can destroy the pair structure that a competing configuration relied on), and its nonlinearity is quadratic, so there is no dual. Fast stirring supplies a small parameter for the hydrodynamic limit, but the hydrodynamic limit is deterministic and cannot distinguish two stationary laws with the same density: the uniqueness question lives entirely in the fluctuation field, which the eps -> 0 limit erases.
result: The block construction gives a two-sided density bound: any stationary distribution nu that is not the all-empty state dominates the upper invariant measure of a supercritical oriented percolation, so nu-a.s. the density is at least some rho_- > 0, and by the same comparison run downwards the density is at most rho_+ < 1, with rho_+ - rho_- tending to 0 as eps -> 0 because both are read off the same PDE steady state. So all nontrivial stationary distributions have the SAME asymptotic density as eps -> 0. That is the honest reach of the standard machinery, and it is strictly weaker than uniqueness: equality of one-dimensional marginals does not determine a measure on {0,1}^{Z^d}. Recording that gap explicitly is the useful output, because it says a proof must add a coupling or a duality, not a sharper density estimate.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The mean-field interior fixed point exists only for p < q and disappears again as p decreases, which is why the conjectured coexistence region is a bounded interval and not a half-line.
method: Ask what the small parameter is doing in each of the two existing proofs and whether either can be made quantitative at a fixed lattice.
obstruction: The block construction needs 'one occupied block makes two', which for a three-state non-attractive system means controlling a two-dimensional density vector, so the finite-box estimate is over a set of configurations rather than a single event, and its probability must be bounded below explicitly. The discontinuity that simulations report at the upper critical value makes matters worse: near p_2 the block estimate degrades as a first-order transition, so no continuity or perturbative argument can reach the edge of the interval, and any proof will produce an interval strictly inside the true one.
result: Both existing proofs buy the same thing: they make the local dynamics close to a deterministic system whose interior fixed point is attracting, so that a single block can be shown to seed its neighbours. Fast stirring does it by a hydrodynamic limit, the N x N polymer by making the vacancy requirement macroscopic. At fixed p, q, r and no stirring there is no small parameter at all, and the only remaining route is a finite-range comparison: exhibit a finite space-time box and a finite set of configurations such that a rigorous estimate on that box (in principle a computer-assisted one, as has been done for other two-dimensional particle systems) shows the block construction's percolation is supercritical. The conjecture's specific shape - an INTERVAL (p_1, p_2) rather than a half-line - is forced by the mean-field structure: the interior fixed point exists only when p < q, and it disappears as p decreases too, so coexistence must be lost at both ends.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For a bistable reaction term g the travelling-wave speed satisfies c times the integral of (w')^2 equals the integral of g between the two stable states, so the sign of the speed is the sign of that integral - the whole conjecture is that this sign is positive when lambda_1 < lambda_2 and the death rates are equal.
method: Take the source's own simulation observation seriously and ask what statement it is evidence for: the two types segregate into large single-type regions and the interface moves. That is an interface problem, not a density problem.
obstruction: The reduction to an interface velocity is rigorous only under fast stirring, where the particle system converges to the PDE. Without a small parameter the interface is rough, its width is of the same order as the lattice spacing, and there is no known way to define its velocity, let alone compare it with the PDE's. The system is also not attractive, so the interface cannot be handled by a monotone comparison with a one-dimensional growth process.
result: Under segregation the long-time behaviour is decided by the sign of the interface velocity, which in the mean-field PDE is the sign of the integral of the reaction term across the connecting orbit - the same computation the source performs for the sexual reproduction model, where c has the sign of the integral of g over the interval between the two stable states. So the conjecture is equivalent to: for lambda_1 < lambda_2 and delta_1 = delta_2 = 1 the corresponding integral is strictly positive, i.e. the colicin advantage always beats the birth-rate disadvantage. This is a scalar computation for the PDE, and it is exactly the content of the mean-field bistability the source reports. What is NOT thereby proved: that the particle system with no stirring segregates at all, or that its interface follows the PDE velocity; those are the two hard steps, and they are what makes the conjecture a conjecture.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The replicator dynamics of a skew-symmetric (zero-sum) invasion matrix conserves prod_i u_i^{c_i}, which is what confines the interior orbits; a general measured tournament matrix has no such invariant, so the five-species problem is not the three-species theorem with more indices.
method: Ask what the word 'cyclic' has to mean here for the known three-species proofs to have any chance of transferring, since Silvertown's matrix is a general nonnegative matrix rather than a cyclic permutation.
obstruction: Multitype systems with q > 3 types have no monotone structure and no duality (the biased voter model with unequal rates is not the voter model, so the coalescing-random-walk dual is lost), and the block construction requires a spreading statement for a five-dimensional reaction-diffusion system whose interior fixed point, for the measured matrix, is a spiral rather than a sink. Spreading for a spiral fixed point is not covered by any general theorem.
result: The three-species proofs use an exact structure that the five-species matrix does not have: for the strictly cyclic system the mean-field replicator dynamics has the conserved quantity prod_i u_i^{c_i} for suitable positive c_i, which is what keeps the interior orbits from spiralling out, and the spatial proof then shows that local spirals stabilise the conserved quantity. For a general tournament matrix such a conserved quantity exists only if the matrix is (after scaling) skew-symmetric on the interior, which is a codimension-positive condition on the 20 entries and is NOT satisfied by Silvertown's measured numbers. So the honest statement is that the conjecture as posed is not the five-species case of the known three-species theorem; it is a different problem, and the 'partial credit' version - coexistence for SOME parameters - is the one for which the conserved-quantity route is available, namely for matrices close to skew-symmetric.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: phi(u) = -sum_i c_i log u_i is convex and blows up on the boundary of the simplex, and is conserved by a zero-sum replicator flow; it is therefore the natural candidate for the survey's own Theorem 5, and the whole question is whether the colicin production cost keeps it nonincreasing.
method: Identify which of the two available coexistence machines applies: the fast-stirring Lyapunov theorem (Theorem 5 of the survey) or the cyclic-structure argument.
obstruction: Whether the required inequality holds for the actual colicin rates is not settled by the survey, and 'coexistence with fast stirring' is weaker than the question, which is posed for the model as given. Removing the stirring runs into the same wall as E0011: no small parameter, and a three-dimensional density vector to control in the block construction.
result: The three-species colicin system is a genuine rock-paper-scissors: the colicin producer beats the sensitive strain, the sensitive strain outgrows the resistant one, and the resistant strain outgrows the producer, because producing colicin is costly. That is the structure under which the cyclic machinery could apply, and it is a better target than the five-species problem E0013. Concretely, the fast-stirring theorem needs a convex phi decreasing along the ODE and blowing up at the boundary; for a zero-sum-like three-species replicator the function phi(u) = -sum c_i log u_i is exactly of that type (it blows up at the boundary and is convex), and it is constant, hence nonincreasing, along the ODE when the interaction is skew-symmetric. So for the skew-symmetric idealisation the survey's own Theorem 5 applies and gives coexistence with fast stirring. The genuine colicin matrix is only approximately skew-symmetric because of the cost of production; the honest conclusion is that Theorem 5 applies to a perturbation only if phi remains nonincreasing, which requires the cost term to have the right sign, and that is a checkable inequality on the model's rates rather than a theorem.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Coexistence here is a rescue effect: the invariant object is not a stationary density but the survival of Doves in the wake of local Hawk crashes, a state the homogeneously-mixing ODE cannot represent at all.
method: Ask what the spatial model has that the ODE does not, in a form that could be turned into a proof, and check the mechanism the source proposes: local crashes followed by recolonisation.
obstruction: The selection here is not small: the payoff entries are order one, so the process is not a voter-model perturbation and the Cox-Durrett-Perkins rescaling does not apply. Without that rescaling the block event has to be verified for a non-attractive two-type system at fixed parameters, which is the same finite-box obstacle as in E0011. The population can also die out globally, so the block construction must be run for a process that is not conservative, and the usual comparison with oriented percolation requires a lower bound on the total mass that no monotonicity supplies.
result: The proposed mechanism is a rescue effect and it has a precise signature: the survival of Doves is a statement about the SURVIVAL OF A SUPERCRITICAL GROWTH PROCESS IN THE DEBRIS OF A CRASH, not about a stationary density. That distinguishes this problem from all the others in the survey, and it explains why the mean-field picture (total extinction) is not merely quantitatively wrong but qualitatively so: the ODE has no state in which one region is empty while another is full, and it is exactly such states that carry the coexistence. The route with content is therefore a two-scale block construction in which the block event is 'a block that is mostly Dove at time 0 produces two mostly-Dove blocks at time T even though Hawks invade and crash inside it'. The small-selection theorems of Cox-Durrett-Perkins reach a nearby statement by a different route (perturbation of the voter model), and the natural first step is to check whether the specific matrix (-0.6, 0.9, -0.9, 0.7) can be reached from the voter model by a path of games along which their phase-diagram criterion stays on the coexistence side.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For a complete non-orthogonal eigenbasis the semigroup bound carries the Riesz constant of the basis as a prefactor, and that constant is the limit of the condition numbers of the Gram matrices of the eigenpolynomials under mu - a computable moment problem here, since the moments m_n are explicit.
method: Ask what 'spectral estimate' can mean for a generator whose eigenvectors are complete but not orthogonal, and test the natural substitute: a Riesz-basis or a similarity-transform bound.
obstruction: The eigenvalues are lambda_n = 1 - 2^{-n}, which accumulate at 1; the spectral gap is therefore fine, but the eigenvalue spacing shrinks geometrically, which is exactly the regime in which non-normal operators have large pseudospectra and the naive spectral bound fails by a factor growing with the truncation. For such generators the semigroup can grow transiently by a factor that swamps the exponential decay for a long time, so a spectral bound without control of the Riesz constant says nothing about finite times, which is what an ergodicity estimate is for.
result: The obstruction is quantitative and can be located exactly. If the polynomial eigenfunctions {P_n} formed a Riesz basis of L^2(mu), the semigroup would satisfy ||P_t f - mu(f)|| <= kappa exp(-lambda_1 t) ||f - mu(f)|| with kappa the Riesz constant, which is the condition number of the change of basis from {P_n} to an orthonormal basis. So the whole question is whether that condition number is finite - and the source's own datum, that the Gram matrix of the P_n has nonzero off-diagonal entries, does not by itself decide this: a basis can be non-orthogonal and still Riesz. What decides it is the growth of the Gram matrix's condition number as the truncation size grows. That is a computable question about a moment matrix determined by the explicit moments m_n, and it is a sharper target than 'use the spectral properties'. It is a reformulation and not a bound: no growth rate is established here.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: G(r) tends to the exponent of the averaged matrix (A_0+A_1)/2 as r -> infinity and to the mean of the two individual exponents as r -> 0, so an interior maximum is free from continuity; unimodality is the entire content of the conjecture.
method: Check the two endpoint claims separately from the unimodality claim, since they have different proofs and different difficulty.
obstruction: G(r) is the top Lyapunov exponent of a random product, which has no closed form and is not known to be even differentiable in r for general pairs (A_0, A_1) - Furstenberg-type formulas give it as an integral of a cocycle against the stationary measure of the induced process on the projective line, and that stationary measure moves with r in a way that is only Holder. Establishing a single sign change of the derivative would need monotonicity of that projective stationary measure in r, and no such monotonicity is known.
result: The two limits are the soft part and follow from averaging at both ends: as r -> infinity the switching averages and the system converges to dX/dt = ((A_0+A_1)/2) X, whose exponent is that of the averaged matrix, and as r -> 0 the process spends long stretches in a single matrix, so the exponent converges to the average of the two individual exponents. The conjecture's G(r) -> 0 at both ends is therefore the statement that the averaged matrix and both individual matrices are stable, which is a check on A_0 and A_1, not a limit theorem. The hard and genuinely open part is the strict unimodality in between - a single sign change of G' - and it is worth recording that unimodality is strictly stronger than the existence of a maximum, which follows from continuity plus the two limits. So the honest decomposition is: existence of an interior maximum is free from the endpoints; uniqueness of the critical point is the whole problem.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Two disjoint instability intervals require two interior local maxima of the Lyapunov exponent as a function of the jump rate; the exponent is the integral of a fixed cocycle against the r-dependent stationary measure on RP^1, so the question is whether that one-parameter family of measures can double back.
method: This is an existence question, so ask what mechanism could produce two disjoint intervals, and whether 2x2 real matrices have enough freedom to supply it.
obstruction: The candidate mechanism is a resonance, and resonances in random switching are typically smoothed: the exponential holding times spread the switching phase uniformly and destroy the locking that would produce a second peak. Making the peak survive needs a nearly deterministic switching schedule, which the exponential clock forbids. Any construction must therefore create the second maximum from the shear rather than the rotation, and the shear contribution to the exponent is monotone in r for the examples in the source.
result: Two disjoint intervals require G(r) - alpha to change sign four times, hence G to have at least two interior local maxima. In the 2x2 case the projective dynamics lives on the circle RP^1, and the switched flow is a random dynamical system on a one-dimensional compact space; the exponent is the integral of a fixed cocycle against a stationary measure that interpolates between the r -> 0 measure (a mixture of the two deterministic invariant measures) and the r -> infinity measure (the invariant measure of the averaged flow). A second local maximum requires this one-parameter family of measures on the circle to double back, i.e. the family cannot be a monotone interpolation. That is possible in principle - two rotation-like matrices with different rotation numbers produce a resonance structure in r - so the natural construction to try is a pair A_0, A_1 whose projective flows are rotations of incommensurate speeds plus small shear. This is a proposed construction, not a verified example: no pair is exhibited here.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: det(A_0 x, A_1 x) = 0 is exactly the set where the two drift fields are collinear and the bracket condition degenerates; the source computes it as -y^2 - yz - alpha z^2 = 0, a pair of lines through the origin.
method: Read the source's own computation as the answer's shape. It computes Q(x) = det(A_0 x, A_1 x) = -y^2 - yz - alpha z^2 and identifies the two lines through the origin where A_0 x and A_1 x are collinear.
obstruction: On the degeneracy lines the invariant measure of a switched flow typically develops a power-law singularity whose exponent is a ratio of the jump rate to the local expansion rate, and that exponent can be less than 1, in which case the density is unbounded and no smoothing argument applies at all. Which side of that threshold the model sits on depends on the pair (r, A_0, A_1) jointly, so there is no dichotomy statement valid for all PDMPs of this class, and a general answer to the question as posed is unlikely to exist.
result: That determinant is the bracket condition made explicit, and it says where regularity can and cannot come for free: off the two lines {Q = 0} the pair (A_0 x, A_1 x) spans the plane, the switched flow satisfies a Hormander-type condition and the invariant density can be expected to be smooth by the standard hypoellipticity route for PDMPs; on the two lines the two drifts are parallel and the smoothing mechanism degenerates. So the honest prediction is not 'the density is smooth' but 'the density is smooth off a finite union of lines through the origin, with the behaviour ON those lines being the real question' - and the source's own algebra already tells one where they are. Explicitly, the two lines are y = lambda_+ z and y = lambda_- z with lambda_pm = (1 pm sqrt(1+4alpha))/(2 alpha), which the source computes for a different purpose. This is a localisation of the question, not a regularity theorem.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For a PDMP with generator Lf = F.grad f + lambda(x)(Kf - f), a Lyapunov function needs lambda(x) times the jump decrease to beat F.grad V; an unbounded rate helps this inequality and an expanding field hurts it, so the two hypotheses in the question act in opposite directions.
method: Test the two standard machines against the two hypotheses that the question deliberately combines: an expanding vector field, and a jump rate that grows without bound.
obstruction: A Lyapunov drift condition gives exponential ergodicity only with a small-set/minorisation condition, and for a time-reversed PDMP the natural small set is a compact region that the reversed flow may leave in finite time without a jump, so the minorisation has to come from the jump kernel alone. With an unbounded rate the process also risks explosion in the reversed direction: infinitely many jumps in finite time, which the forward process avoided by construction but the reversal need not.
result: They do not fail for the same reason, and separating them is the useful output. A Wasserstein contraction argument fails on the expanding field alone: the flow separates two coupled copies at rate given by the field's positive exponent, and jumps must beat that, which they can only do if the jump kernel is contracting at a rate exceeding the expansion - a condition on the pair, not on either. A Lyapunov (Meyn-Tweedie) argument, by contrast, is actually HELPED by an unbounded jump rate: with rate lambda(x) -> infinity as |x| -> infinity, the generator applied to a test function V growing at infinity acquires a strongly negative term lambda(x)(EV(jump) - V(x)) far out, which dominates the expansion of the field if lambda grows faster than the field's linear rate. So the honest reading is that the two hypotheses push in opposite directions, and the tractable regime is precisely lambda(x) growing superlinearly, where a Lyapunov function should exist. What is not claimed: no drift condition is verified here for the source's Examples 4.6 and 4.7.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For run-and-tumble in R^3 the mixing comes from the commutator of v.grad_x with the tumbling operator on S^2; a spectral gap for the tumbling kernel plus a confining field is what makes it quantitative, and a path-dependent (memory) tumbling rate destroys the gap in the memory coordinate.
method: Ask what is genuinely three-dimensional about the difficulty, since the one-dimensional telegraph process has sharp rates by coupling.
obstruction: Realistic chemotaxis models make the tumbling rate depend on the time derivative of the chemoattractant concentration along the trajectory, which adds an internal memory variable. The resulting process is Markov only on an enlarged state space, and on that space the tumbling operator no longer has a spectral gap in the memory direction, so the hypocoercivity commutator argument has nothing to work with in that coordinate.
result: The difficulty is not dimension per se but the geometry of the velocity space. In one dimension the velocity takes two values and a coupling can be built by making the two copies' velocities agree after a single common tumble; in R^3 the velocity lives on the sphere, tumbles are drawn from a kernel on S^2, and two copies at different positions must be brought to the same velocity AND the same position, which a single tumble cannot do. The right substitute is a hypocoercivity estimate in a weighted H^1-type norm on position-velocity space, where the mixing comes from the commutator of the transport operator with the tumbling operator. This says the tractable structural hypothesis is a spectral gap for the tumbling kernel on S^2 plus a confining external field, and identifies which of the source's 'more realistic' features (a chemotactic tumbling rate depending on the gradient along the path) breaks it: a path-dependent rate makes the process non-Markov in (position, velocity) alone and no operator formulation is available.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Polarity is an energy condition against Re[(alpha + psi(z))^{-1}] over all of z-space; a subspace projection integrates only a slice of that kernel, so the family of projections is strictly less information than the full exponent.
method: Fix the direction that is free. The source's Lemma 3.1 gives the easy implication: if some projection fails (H) then X fails (H). The question is the converse, so ask whether polarity for X can be detected from polarity for all projections.
obstruction: The dichotomy is controlled by how Im(psi) is dominated by 1 + Re(psi) (Kanda-Forst, Rao, and the survey's own C_log conditions). Restricting psi to a subspace can only make the domination easier, since both parts are restricted together, so good behaviour of every restriction is strictly weaker information than good behaviour of psi - there are directions in z-space (not aligned with any subspace restriction in a useful way) along which Im(psi) could escape. Constructing such an exponent, or showing none exists, is the actual work.
result: It cannot, at the level of the underlying capacity theory, and that is the relevant warning. Polarity for a Levy process is an energy condition against the kernel Re[(alpha + psi(z))^{-1}] (the source's own alpha-energy), and the projected process has exponent psi restricted to the subspace, so the projected energy integrates over a lower-dimensional slice of z-space. A set can be non-polar for X (positive capacity) while every projection is polar, and conversely, for the same reason that a compact set in the plane can have positive Hausdorff dimension while its projections in a family of directions are null - the projection of a measure controls only the slice of its Fourier transform along that direction. So the honest content of Question 1 is not 'can projections see polarity' (they cannot in general) but the weaker 'can projections see the semipolar-versus-polar DICHOTOMY', which is a statement about the structure of the exponent rather than about individual sets. Recording that distinction is the useful step; it does not answer the question.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The survey's counterexample fails (H) through a single degenerate line on which the process becomes uniform motion; quantifying over all lines removes that mechanism, leaving only the pure-jump case as genuinely open.
method: Take the source's counterexample to Question 3 and ask how far it can be pushed, since Question 2 differs from Question 3 only by enlarging the family of directions tested.
obstruction: For a pure-jump process there is no matrix Q whose rank identifies the bad directions; the analogue is the set of directions in which the Levy measure's projection has finite variation and the projected process is a drift plus a compound Poisson process. Whether that set can be empty in every direction while (H) still fails for X is exactly the open case, and no invariant of the Levy measure is known that detects it.
result: The counterexample is X_t = a t + sqrt(Q) B_t with Q = [[2,2],[2,2]] and a = (1,-1): each coordinate-axis projection has a nondegenerate Gaussian part and so satisfies (H), but the projection onto the line {y = -x} is a uniform motion, which fails (H), and hence X fails (H) by Lemma 3.1. This shows the mechanism precisely: the failure is a DEGENERATE DIRECTION, a line on which the Gaussian part vanishes and only a drift survives. Question 2 forbids exactly that, since it tests every line including the degenerate one. So Question 2 has content only for processes with no degenerate direction of uniform-motion type, and for the Gaussian-plus-drift family it is therefore TRUE by Theorem 2.5 of the same survey (nondegenerate Q implies (H)). The residual open case is the purely non-Gaussian one, where 'degenerate direction' is not visible from Q. That reduction is the useful output.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: psi_{(X_1,X_2)}(z_1,z_2) = psi_1(z_1) + psi_2(z_2): Re adds and |Im| is subadditive, so any sufficient condition of the form |Im psi| <= (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi) with f increasing survives the sum up to replacing f by 2f.
method: Push the survey's own Proposition 3.10 mechanism as far as it goes. The exponent of the product is psi(z_1, z_2) = psi_1(z_1) + psi_2(z_2), so Re and Im are additive; ask which of the known sufficient conditions for (H) is stable under that addition.
obstruction: The survey's weaker sufficient conditions (EKFR, C_log, C_log-log) are quantified over finite measures of finite 1-energy, with a measure-dependent sequence y_k. Under addition of exponents the level sets {y_k <= B(z) < y_k^beta} of B = 1 + Re(psi) change shape in the product space, and a measure on R^{n+m} of finite energy need not factor, so there is no way to produce the required sequence for the product from the two given sequences. That is exactly where the additivity argument stops.
result: Kanda-Forst is stable, which is what Proposition 3.10 uses, and so is Rao's strictly larger class, which the survey does not observe. Rao's condition is |Im(psi)| <= (1 + Re(psi)) f(1 + Re(psi)) with f increasing on [1, infinity) and the integral of 1/(lambda f(lambda)) divergent. If psi_1 and psi_2 both satisfy it with the same f, then using 1 + Re(psi_i) <= 1 + Re(psi) and monotonicity of f, |Im psi| <= |Im psi_1| + |Im psi_2| <= (2 + Re psi_1 + Re psi_2) f(1 + Re psi) <= 2 (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi), so psi satisfies Rao's condition with f replaced by 2f, and the divergence of the integral of 1/(2 lambda f(lambda)) is unaffected. Resolvent densities pass to the product because a convolution with a density is a density. Hence: the answer to Question 4 is YES for every pair of processes in Rao's class. This is a genuine extension of Proposition 3.10 and it is easy; it is emphatically NOT an answer to the question as posed, because the survey's whole point (its Theorems 2.8, 2.11, 2.12) is that (H) holds for processes outside Rao's class.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For a driftless subordinator with stable density of index alpha, Im psi / Re psi tends to tan(pi alpha / 2), a finite constant - Kanda-Forst holds; the type-(alpha,beta) class is precisely the class where that ratio need not have a limit.
method: Compute the shape of the exponent for a subordinator and see what the Kanda-Forst ratio looks like, since that ratio is the only quantity all the known sufficient conditions control.
obstruction: To exploit the oscillation one has to control Re psi from below along the sparse sequence where Im psi is large, and the two-sided bound c^{-1} x^{-(1+alpha)} <= nu <= c x^{-(1+beta)} does not force Re psi to be regularly varying, so no Tauberian theorem applies. The survey's own weaker conditions require choosing a sequence y_k adapted to each measure of finite energy, which is why Theorem 2.29 covers only a subclass.
result: For a driftless subordinator the exponent is psi(z) = integral over (0, infinity) of (1 - e^{i z x}) nu(dx), so Re psi(z) = integral (1 - cos(zx)) nu(dx) and Im psi(z) = -integral sin(zx) nu(dx). Both integrands are supported on the same scales, and for a stable-like nu(dx) = x^{-(1+alpha)} dx a scaling computation gives Re psi(z) asymptotically c_alpha |z|^alpha and Im psi(z) asymptotically c_alpha tan(pi alpha / 2) |z|^alpha, so the ratio |Im psi| / (1 + Re psi) is BOUNDED and Kanda-Forst holds - which is why all stable subordinators satisfy (H). The type-(alpha,beta) case is exactly the case where the two-sided bound allows the mass to oscillate between the two scaling exponents, so Re psi can dip along a sparse sequence of z while Im psi does not, and the ratio can be unbounded. This identifies the mechanism precisely: the difficulty is not infinite activity, it is a Levy density with oscillating scaling, and a subordinator whose density has a genuine limit exponent is in Kanda-Forst and hence satisfies (H). This is a description of where the open case lives; it does not settle it.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Splitting a Levy process at a jump scale writes it as an independent sum of a small-jump part and a compound Poisson part; the latter has bounded exponent and satisfies Kanda-Forst, and Rao's class is closed under independent sums, so only the small-jump part can obstruct (H).
method: Use the survey's own reduction (Question 7 implies Question 6, via Kesten's Theorem 1(f)) together with a stability observation for Rao's class.
obstruction: The reduction is only as good as Rao's condition, and the survey's own point is that (H) can hold outside it; conversely the infinite-variation hypothesis in Question 6 does not by itself force any lower bound on Re psi, so it does not force the ratio to be bounded. Getoor's conjecture, which subsumes this question, has been open for fifty years.
result: Combining the two gives a concrete class in which Question 6 has a positive answer. By the argument recorded in E0024, Rao's sufficient condition |Im psi| <= (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi) with f increasing and the integral of 1/(lambda f(lambda)) divergent is stable under independent sums up to replacing f by 2f. Hence any one-dimensional Levy process that DECOMPOSES as an independent sum of processes each in Rao's class is itself in Rao's class and satisfies (H). Since a process with infinite jump variation can always be split at a scale into a small-jump part and a large-jump (compound Poisson) part, and compound Poisson processes have bounded exponent hence trivially satisfy Kanda-Forst, the question reduces to the SMALL-JUMP part alone: Question 6 holds whenever the small-jump component satisfies Rao's condition. That is a genuine reduction (the large-jump part is never the obstruction), and it is not an answer, since the small-jump part is exactly where an oscillating Levy density can break the ratio.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For independent summands Re psi adds and |Im psi| is subadditive, so every sufficient condition for (H) of the pointwise form |Im psi| <= (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi) with f increasing is closed under independent sums, up to replacing f by 2f.
method: Test each of the known sufficient conditions for (H) for stability under addition of the Levy-Khintchine exponents, since psi_{X+Y} = psi_X + psi_Y for independent summands.
obstruction: The survey's own weaker conditions (EKFR, C_log, C_log-log) are not of the pointwise form |Im psi| <= g(Re psi): they involve, for each finite measure of finite 1-energy, an integral over the level sets of B = 1 + Re psi against |Fourier transform of mu|^2 and a measure-dependent sequence y_k. Adding exponents moves those level sets, and no relation between the sequences for psi_X, psi_Y and one for psi is available. So the residual open case is exactly the pair where at least one summand satisfies (H) only through a measure-dependent condition.
result: Kanda-Forst is stable: if |Im psi_X| <= M(1 + Re psi_X) and |Im psi_Y| <= M(1 + Re psi_Y) then |Im psi| <= M(2 + Re psi_X + Re psi_Y) <= 2M(1 + Re psi). Rao's condition is also stable, with the same argument as in E0024: monotonicity of f and 1 + Re psi_i <= 1 + Re psi give |Im psi| <= 2(1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi), and the required divergence of the integral of 1/(lambda f(lambda)) is unaffected by the factor 2; the sum has resolvent densities as soon as one summand does. So the answer to Question 7 is YES whenever both summands lie in Rao's class - a class strictly larger than Kanda-Forst and containing all stable processes and every process with a nondegenerate Gaussian part. The survey does not record this. The caveat matters and is the reason this is not an answer: the survey's Theorems 2.8, 2.11 and 2.12 exist precisely because (H) holds for processes OUTSIDE Rao's class, and for those the argument gives nothing.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: An exponential tilt of n i.i.d. coordinates by delta has total variation cost of order delta sqrt(n) and shifts an additive functional by order delta n; delta = n^{-1/2} makes the cost O(1) and the shift sqrt(n), which is the method's calibration.
method: Read off what the distribution classes are doing in the method. The engine is the source's Lemma 1.2: for X and Y on a common space, P(a <= X <= b) <= (1/2)(1 + P(|X-Y| <= b-a) + d_TV(L_X, L_Y)). One needs a coupled perturbation Y that is cheap in total variation but moves X by the conjectured fluctuation scale.
obstruction: For discrete weights the only available perturbations are resamplings, which change the total variation by an amount bounded below by the atom sizes, so one cannot make the cost o(1) while moving the functional. That is the same wall as item (6) of the same list (discrete edge weights in first-passage percolation), so the general problem and the discrete problem are one obstruction, not two.
result: The role of P(d) and P+(d) is to make a TILT of the underlying product measure both admissible and computable: for i.i.d. coordinates tilted by a parameter delta, the total variation cost of n coordinates is of order delta sqrt(n) and the induced shift of a Lipschitz functional is of order delta n times its mean sensitivity. Setting delta = c n^{-1/2} makes the cost O(1), which is exactly the requirement of Lemma 1.2, and produces a fluctuation lower bound of the order of the resulting shift. So the hypotheses are not about the functional at all; they are about the existence of an exponential-family tilt with a computable Hellinger cost. The minimal-assumption version of the problem is therefore: for which laws mu on the coordinates does there exist a one-parameter family mu_delta with H^2(mu, mu_delta) = O(delta^2) and a monotone effect on the functional? For any mu with a nondegenerate absolutely continuous part this is available; the genuinely hard case is a lattice mu with atoms, where a tilt cannot move the support.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For a stabilising functional the variance converges to an explicit Poisson add-one-cost integral, and Steele's constant would be that integral; the whole conjecture is that the TSP tour stabilises.
method: Ask what structure would make a variance converge, and check whether the TSP functional has it. Convergence of Var to a constant is what a functional with a local (stabilizing) representation does, via an add-one-cost martingale decomposition.
obstruction: The TSP is not known to stabilise. The best available locality statement is that the optimal tour is close to optimal on cells of a partition (the boundary-functional method of Redmond and Yukich), which controls the mean to O(sqrt(n)) but leaves an error in the variance of the same order as the variance itself. Making the boundary error o(1) requires an estimate on the number of tour edges crossing a fixed line, which is what nobody can control.
result: The natural route is stabilisation: if the tour length admits a representation as a sum over points of a local add-one cost that depends only on a neighbourhood of radius O_P(1) after rescaling to intensity one, then the Penrose-Yukich central limit theorem gives both a CLT and convergence of the normalised variance to a constant expressed as an integral of a two-point add-one correlation over the Poisson process. The identification of Steele's constant is then automatic in the same formula. So the conjecture is a stabilisation statement, and its difficulty is exactly that the TSP tour is a GLOBAL constraint: inserting a point can reroute the tour arbitrarily far away. The known partial substitutes - Rhee-Talagrand concentration - bound the variance from above by a constant but do not establish stabilisation, and an upper bound of constant order plus the source's lower bound of constant order still leaves the limit unproven.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Minimal matching of n uniform points has mean cost of order n^{1-1/d} for d >= 3 but n^{1/2}(log n)^{1/2} in d = 2, and the d = 2 cost is governed by a log-correlated field, so the fluctuation problem splits into a local and a field-level case.
method: Use the dimension dependence to decide what 'tight' should mean, since the answer is not the same in all d. For n uniform points in [0,1]^d the minimal matching cost has mean of order n^{1-1/d} for d >= 3 and n^{1/2} (log n)^{1/2} in d = 2.
obstruction: In d = 2 the field-level heuristic predicts fluctuations of order (log n)^{1/2} for the total cost, which is smaller than the mean by a factor n^{1/2}, so any tilt used in Lemma 1.2 must move the cost by only (log n)^{1/2} while costing O(1) in total variation - an extremely fine calibration, and one that the crude n^{-1/2} tilt of the source's Bernoulli example cannot supply.
result: In d >= 3 the matching cost is a sum of n contributions each of order n^{-1/d}, and the local structure is genuinely local (the optimal matching is stabilising in the sense that a point is matched within distance O(n^{-1/d}) with a stretched-exponential tail), which is why a central limit theorem is expected and the fluctuation order should be n^{1/2 - 1/d}. In d = 2 the matching is NOT local - the Ambrosio-Stra-Trevisan analysis shows the cost is governed by the Gaussian free field at all scales, and the fluctuation order should then be read off from the field, not from a sum of local terms. So 'tight lower bound' means two different theorems in the two regimes, and the source's list does not separate them. That separation is the useful output: the source's coupling method should be calibrated against a local tilt in d >= 3 and against a global (field-level) tilt in d = 2.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: At the uniform letter distribution the derivative of the mean LCS with respect to a frequency tilt vanishes by symmetry, so a tilt of total variation cost O(1) moves the LCS by O(1) rather than by sqrt(n); the method's calibration fails at first order precisely at the symmetric point.
method: Ask why uniformity is the hard case rather than the easy one, since it is the most symmetric.
obstruction: To recover a first-order effect at the symmetric point one must tilt in a direction that is not a frequency change - for instance, a correlation between the two words - but any such tilt breaks the independence of the two sequences, and then the total variation cost is no longer a product-measure computation. This is the same difficulty as constructing a non-product perturbation in item (1).
result: Because the method needs an asymmetry to tilt. For non-uniform letter distributions one perturbs the letter frequencies: raising the probability of the most common letter increases the expected LCS at a computable rate, and the total variation cost of the tilt is controlled - exactly the calibration of item (1). Under the uniform distribution the first-order effect of any frequency tilt VANISHES by symmetry (the derivative of the LCS mean with respect to a symmetric perturbation of the simplex is zero at the symmetric point), so the leading term of the shift is second order in delta while the cost stays first order, and the calibration delta = n^{-1/2} that made the method work now gives a shift of order n^{1/2} times delta = O(1) rather than the required sqrt(n). This identifies the exact reason uniform letters resist the method, which the source records only as 'the most important case is open'.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A uniform tilt over the n^2 edges of the box has cost delta n and moves the passage time by delta n, giving only O(1) at unit cost; an efficient tilt must charge the O(n) edges on the geodesic, and locating them is the transversal fluctuation problem.
method: Compare the achieved order with the calibration of Lemma 1.2 to see what an improvement would require.
obstruction: Any geodesic-adapted perturbation is a function of the very randomness being perturbed, so the two laws in Lemma 1.2 are not related by a fixed change of measure. Circumventing this needs a two-step argument in which the geodesic is localised first, which is precisely the transversal-fluctuation problem (exponent xi), itself open in d = 2.
result: The sqrt(log n) bound is exactly what a tilt supported on the whole box gives: the passage time to distance n depends on order n^2 edges, a uniform tilt of size delta costs delta n in total variation, so delta = 1/n, and the shift produced by such a tilt is delta times the number of edges ON the geodesic, i.e. delta times n, which is O(1) - the sqrt(log n) comes from summing scales dyadically. To reach n^{1/3} one must tilt only the edges near the geodesic, of which there are order n, giving a cost delta sqrt(n) and a shift delta n, hence a shift of sqrt(n) at unit cost - too big, so the true constraint is that the tilt must be chosen adapted to the geodesic and the adaptivity destroys the product structure. This says the barrier is not the size of the tilt but its MEASURABILITY: an efficient tilt must know where the geodesic is, and then L_Y is no longer a product measure and d_TV is not computable.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Resampling each edge independently with probability eps has total variation cost of order eps times the number of edges and shifts the passage time by at most eps times the geodesic length, so the shift-to-cost ratio survives discreteness; what fails is that the shift has random sign.
method: Identify the exact failure of the coupling for atoms, and look for a substitute perturbation that is available in the discrete case.
obstruction: Recovering the sign needs a positive-probability event on which the resampling raises the passage time by a definite amount, which in turn needs a lower bound on the number of pivotal edges of the geodesic - and the number of pivotals is exactly the quantity whose fluctuation one is trying to bound. Newman-Piza avoid this by working with the variance rather than the concentration function, which is why their result exists for {0,1} weights and the fluctuation-order statement does not.
result: With continuous weights the perturbation is a small shift of each weight, whose total variation cost is proportional to the shift; with weights on a lattice the smallest available move is a resampling, whose cost is bounded below by a constant times the number of resampled edges divided by nothing - i.e. resampling m edges costs an amount of order m p, where p is the smallest atom, and this cannot be made o(1) unless m is bounded. The substitute that remains available is a RANDOM-CLUSTER style perturbation: change the weight of each edge independently with probability eps and, on the changed edges, resample. Then d_TV is at most eps times the number of edges, and the shift of the passage time is at most eps times the geodesic length. The ratio shift/cost is then the same as in the continuous case, so the method's calibration is NOT lost by discreteness; what is lost is the monotone control of the shift, since a resampled edge can lower as well as raise the passage time and the effects cancel to first order. The honest conclusion is that discreteness costs the SIGN, not the size, of the perturbation.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A box of side L in Z^d carries of order L^{d-1} edge-disjoint crossings, so tilting one crossing is diluted by L^{d-2}; the exponent d-2 is exactly the gap between the two-dimensional argument and higher dimensions.
method: Ask why the two-dimensional dyadic-scale argument does not simply repeat in d = 3.
obstruction: To beat the dilution one needs to perturb a whole cutset rather than a path, and a cutset in d dimensions has L^{d-1} edges, so the total variation cost of tilting it grows like delta L^{(d-1)/2}, while the induced shift is only delta times the local weight change on the crossing actually used. The ratio degrades with d, and no substitute perturbation with a better ratio is known.
result: The two-dimensional sqrt(log n) comes from summing an O(1) contribution over the log n dyadic scales, and each scale contributes because a box of side 2^k contains a bottleneck that the geodesic must cross and whose weight can be tilted. In d >= 3 the geodesic can go AROUND a perturbed region at a cost that is second order in the perturbation, because the box has many more disjoint crossings: the number of edge-disjoint paths across a box of side L in d dimensions is of order L^{d-1}, so the effect of tilting a fixed fraction of one crossing is diluted by L^{d-2}. That dilution factor, which is 1 in d = 2 and grows in d >= 3, is precisely why the same argument gives only O(1) in higher dimensions. Naming the dilution exponent d-2 is the useful step, and it predicts that the method as it stands cannot produce more than a constant in any d >= 3 without a new idea, rather than merely being unproved there.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Newman-Piza's power-law lower bound uses curvature of the limit shape only through asymptotic disjointness of geodesics to angularly separated endpoints, which is strictly weaker than strict convexity.
method: Separate the conditional from the unconditional statement, since Newman-Piza's power bound is conditional on curvature of the limit shape.
obstruction: Even the weaker disjointness statement is unproven: the only unconditional information about the limit shape in d = 2 is that it is convex, compact, and has the lattice symmetries, and it is not known to be strictly convex anywhere, or differentiable anywhere except at the boundary of the percolation cone.
result: The whole difficulty is that the two available routes need opposite inputs. The curvature route gives chi' > 0 but assumes a strictly convex limit shape - a statement about the shape that nobody can prove for any nondegenerate weight distribution in d = 2. The coupling route (the source's) is unconditional but gives only sqrt(log n). A third possibility, and the one worth stating, is that curvature is not needed in full: the Newman-Piza argument uses curvature only to guarantee that geodesics to nearby endpoints are asymptotically disjoint, and that disjointness is a weaker statement than curvature. Reformulating the required input as 'geodesics to two endpoints at angular separation theta are disjoint outside a ball of radius o(n)' is a strictly weaker hypothesis than strict convexity and is the natural target. This is a reformulation of the hypothesis, not a removal of it.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The coupling route's dilution L^{d-2} grows with d and the curvature route's disjointness input weakens with d, so no known method improves with dimension; and above the conjectured critical dimension chi is expected to vanish, so the statement cannot hold for all d.
method: Combine the dilution computation of E0035 with the curvature route of E0036 and see which one degrades faster in d.
obstruction: There is no dimension in which both the shape input and the disjointness input are available. Above the conjectured critical dimension the fluctuations are expected to be Gaussian with chi = 0, so a proof of chi' > 0 valid in ALL d >= 3 would be false if that prediction is right - the problem as stated is therefore implicitly restricted to d below the (unknown) critical dimension, and identifying that dimension is itself open.
result: They degrade in opposite ways, which is the point worth recording. The curvature route needs less as d grows in one respect - the limit shape in high d is expected to be closer to a ball, hence more plausibly strictly convex - but the geodesic-disjointness input needs more, because two geodesics in d dimensions have more room to run alongside each other without meeting, so angular separation no longer forces disjointness in any quantitative way. The coupling route degrades monotonically in d by the dilution factor L^{d-2}. So neither route improves with dimension, and the natural conjecture chi' > 0 in all d has no method behind it at all - which distinguishes item (9) from item (8), where at least a conditional theorem exists.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A Gaussian tilt of the SK disorder of size delta costs delta N in total variation and shifts the free energy by delta times a Gibbs-averaged energy; in the replica-symmetry-breaking phase that average is not concentrated, so the shift is as random as the quantity being bounded.
method: Ask what the conjectured order is in each phase, since 'optimal' means different things above and below the critical temperature, and check which phase the coupling method can see.
obstruction: In the low-temperature phase the response of the free energy to a disorder perturbation is a Gibbs average over a non-concentrated overlap distribution, so the shift in Lemma 1.2 is itself random of the same order as the fluctuation being bounded. Breaking that circularity requires control of the overlap distribution at the level of its fluctuations, which is what the Parisi formula does not give.
result: Above criticality the free energy has Gaussian fluctuations of order 1/N (in the normalisation where the free energy is O(1) per spin), and the coupling method's tilt - perturbing the disorder matrix by an independent Gaussian of size delta - costs delta N in total variation and shifts the free energy by delta times the overlap-weighted energy, so the calibration reproduces the right order. Below criticality the conjectured order is N^{-5/6} times a Tracy-Widom-type law for the ground state, and the source's method cannot see it because the shift of the free energy under a tilt is governed by the Gibbs average of the perturbation, which in the replica-symmetry-breaking phase is not concentrated. So the honest statement is that the method is calibrated in the phase where the answer is already known and blind in the phase where the question is open.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Tilting n^2 i.i.d. exponential costs by delta costs of order delta n in total variation and shifts the optimal assignment cost by order delta, so the shift-to-cost calibration is exactly critical at the conjectured fluctuation scale 1/n.
method: Use the exactly solvable structure, which this problem has and the others on the list do not. For exponential costs the expected optimal assignment cost on K_{n,n} is exactly the sum over k <= n of 1/k^2, and Wastlund's method computes it by a recursive exact identity.
obstruction: The telescoping increments are strongly negatively correlated (adding a row makes the next row's marginal gain smaller), so the variance of the sum is much smaller than the sum of the variances and cannot be estimated term by term. The source's coupling method needs a tilt that moves the cost by n^{-1} at unit total variation cost, and a tilt of n^2 exponential costs by delta costs delta n and moves the assignment cost by delta, giving delta = 1/n and a shift of 1/n - so the calibration is exactly critical here, which explains why the source obtains the right order but not optimality.
result: The exact formula fixes the mean but not the variance, and the reason is structural: Wastlund's recursion computes an EXPECTATION by an exchangeability argument that does not lift to second moments, because the increments it telescopes are not independent. The conjectured fluctuation order is n^{-1} (so that the cost is zeta(2) + Theta(1/n)), which coincides with the order of the largest single term of the exact sum - and that coincidence is the natural target: prove that the fluctuation is dominated by the last few terms of the telescoping. This gives a concrete route that the source's list does not name, and it is a route, not a proof.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A random Toeplitz matrix has only order n independent entries, so a tilt costs delta sqrt(n) rather than delta n; the shift it induces on the spectrum is governed by the symbol-to-spectrum Jacobian, which is singular at the spectral edge.
method: Split the request into its two halves, because they have opposite difficulty profiles: linear statistics are smooth functionals of the whole spectrum, extreme eigenvalues are non-smooth functionals of its edge.
obstruction: Patterned ensembles have order n independent entries but n^2 matrix entries, so the entries are heavily dependent and the total variation cost of a tilt is computed on the wrong space; the shift, in contrast, lives on the matrix. Reconciling the two requires the Jacobian of the map from symbol to spectrum, which for Toeplitz matrices is singular at the edge - precisely where the extreme-eigenvalue question lives.
result: For linear statistics the coupling method is well calibrated: a Gaussian tilt of the n independent entries of a Toeplitz matrix (there are only order n of them, not n^2) costs delta sqrt(n) and shifts a linear statistic by order delta n times the derivative of the test function, so delta = n^{-1/2} gives a shift of sqrt(n) - and since linear statistics of patterned ensembles have fluctuations of order 1 (no n^{1/2} normalisation), the method is far from tight and the correct calibration must exploit cancellation. For extreme eigenvalues the shift under a rank-one-like tilt is bounded by the tilt's operator norm, which for a Toeplitz perturbation of size delta is delta times sqrt(n log n), so the method predicts fluctuations of at least n^{-1/2} times that, i.e. of order sqrt(log n) - almost certainly not tight. Recording that the two halves need different calibrations, and that the linear-statistics half is the one where the method overshoots, is the useful output.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The six examples split into stabilising ones, where a Gaussian limit would follow from an add-one-cost decomposition, and first-passage percolation, where the expected limit is Tracy-Widom and no decomposition into asymptotically independent pieces can exist.
method: Ask what a distributional limit needs beyond a matching pair of bounds, and identify which example is closest.
obstruction: For the stabilising candidates the missing ingredient is stabilisation itself (see E0030 and E0031). For first-passage percolation a Tracy-Widom limit is currently only reachable through exact solvability, which nearest-neighbour first-passage percolation does not have; every known Tracy-Widom result in the KPZ class uses a determinantal or Yang-Baxter structure absent here.
result: A limit law needs an approximate decomposition of the functional into asymptotically independent pieces. Of the six examples, the one with such a decomposition in sight is minimal matching in d >= 3, where the optimal matching is expected to stabilise and the Penrose-Yukich machinery would give a Gaussian limit outright; the source's own list separates matching (item 3) from the limit-theorem request (item 13) but the two are the same theorem in that dimension range. In first-passage percolation the expected limit is not Gaussian but Tracy-Widom, so no decomposition into independent pieces can exist and the request is of a completely different nature there. Pointing out that item (13) is really two requests - a Gaussian one for the stabilising examples and an integrable one for first-passage percolation - is the useful separation.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Under ||u_i||_2 <= 1 the total coordinate variance is at most n but may concentrate in one coordinate, so random signs give only sqrt(n log n); the conjecture is a convex-geometry statement, not a concentration statement.
method: Test what the probabilistic (random signs) benchmark gives and how far it is from the conjecture, so that the gap being attacked is explicit.
obstruction: Banaszczyk's theorem produces a signing into any convex body of Gaussian measure at least 1/2 after scaling by 5; the cube of side sqrt(log n) is the smallest such cube, and the Gaussian measure threshold is what forces the logarithm. Removing it requires a balancing result for a body of small Gaussian measure, which the transference argument cannot give.
result: Random signs give, for each coordinate j, a sum of independent terms with variance sum_i u_i(j)^2, and the constraint ||u_i||_2 <= 1 bounds the sum over j of that variance by n, not each coordinate individually. So the worst case for random signs is all the mass in one coordinate: variance n, giving max coordinate of order sqrt(n log n) - the trivial bound. This is worth recording because it shows the conjecture is not a concentration statement at all: any proof must be a genuine partial colouring / convex-geometric argument, and the probabilistic method is off by a factor of sqrt(n log n), not by a logarithm. Banaszczyk's sqrt(log n) already exploits the convex body, and the remaining gap is exactly one square root of a logarithm.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For rank-one A_i = v_i v_i^T every ordered product collapses to a chain of inner products times v_first v_last^T, which makes both averages explicit and turns the conjecture into a comparison of two weighted word sums.
method: Check whether the two directions can both be false, or whether one direction is forced, by testing the commuting case and a rank-one case.
obstruction: The rank-one reduction makes both sides computable but the normalisations differ, and the tiny-vector construction may violate the implicit assumption that the A_i are comparable. A proper check needs the exact inequality with both normalisations at n = 4 or 5, which is a finite semidefinite feasibility problem of the same kind Lai and Lim solved for direction (a).
