result: When the A_i commute both sides are the same product of scalars in different orders and the two conjectures both hold with equality on the spectrum, so no commuting example distinguishes them - which is why the problem is genuinely noncommutative. For rank-one A_i = v_i v_i^T the products telescope: A_{k_1}...A_{k_n} = (prod of inner products) v_{k_1} v_{k_n}^T, so both averages become explicit sums over words weighted by chains of inner products, and direction (b) asserts that the permutation average of such chains dominates the free average. Since permutations force all n vectors to appear exactly once while the free average is dominated by the single repeated word with the largest self-overlap, direction (b) is FALSE on rank-one examples with one dominant vector: taking v_1 = e_1 and v_2,...,v_n tiny makes the free average of order ||v_1||^{2n} while every permutation product contains all the tiny vectors. This is a candidate refutation, stated as such - I have not verified the constants, and the correct comparison requires the two normalisations 1/n! and 1/n^n to be handled carefully, so it should be checked before being believed.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For d = 1 the objective depends on the basis only through the variance vector (v_i^T Sigma v_i), and the eigenbasis is its majorisation-extreme point; for d >= 2 it depends on the joint law of subset sums, which the variance vector does not determine.
method: Isolate why d = 1 is easy and what breaks at d = 2, by writing the objective as an expected maximum over subsets.
obstruction: The eigenbasis makes the coordinates independent, which maximises the spread of the subset sums but minimises their positive correlation; for d >= 2 the expected maximum over subsets can be increased by correlation, and the two effects pull in opposite directions with no known comparison. A counterexample, if one exists, will be a basis mixing the top eigenvectors so that several subsets are simultaneously large.
result: For d = 1 the objective is E max_i (v_i^T g)^2, a maximum of p correlated squared Gaussians with variances v_i^T Sigma v_i summing to trace(Sigma). Since a maximum of Gaussians is maximised by making the variances as UNEQUAL as possible under a fixed sum, and the eigenbasis is the unique basis realising the extreme point of the majorisation order on the variance vector, the d = 1 case is a Schur-convexity statement. For d >= 2 the objective is the maximum over subsets of SUMS of d such squares, and the relevant vector of subset-variances is no longer the image of the basis under a fixed linear map: two different bases can give the same multiset of individual variances but different subset sums, because the correlations between the (v_i^T g)^2 differ. So the d = 1 proof does not degrade quantitatively at d = 2 - it fails structurally, because Schur convexity in the variance vector is no longer the right order. Naming the correct order (majorisation on the vector of subset variances, which is not determined by the individual variances) is the useful step.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The average singular value of n^{-1/2} X converges to the first absolute moment of the quarter-circle law, 8/(3 pi); the conjecture asserts monotone decrease to that limit, so it entails the one-sided bound E[sigma-bar(n)] > 8/(3 pi) for every n.
method: Compare with the limit, since the quantity converges and the conjecture is that the convergence is one-sided.
obstruction: The Laguerre-kernel expression for E[sigma-bar] is not a ratio of Gamma functions alone - it involves a sum over the n Laguerre polynomials - so the n to n+1 comparison is not termwise, and the standard tool (interlacing of the singular values of X and of X with a row removed) compares the n x n and n x (n+1) ensembles, not the n x n and (n+1) x (n+1) ones with the differing n^{-1/2} normalisation.
result: The average singular value of n^{-1/2} X converges to the first absolute moment of the quarter-circle law, which is 8/(3 pi) = 0.8488..., so monotone decreasing to that limit is the conjecture's content and any proof must therefore show the finite-n value EXCEEDS 8/(3 pi) for every n, which is already a nontrivial one-sided statement. The natural exact route is the known finite-n formula: for the complex Ginibre ensemble the squared singular values are the eigenvalues of a complex Wishart matrix with a Laguerre-ensemble joint density, and E[average singular value] is a single integral against the Laguerre kernel, hence a ratio of Gamma functions and a hypergeometric term. Monotonicity in n then becomes an inequality between two explicit hypergeometric expressions, which is a finite computation in principle. Recording this as the route is the useful output; I have not carried out the hypergeometric comparison.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Rank-r psd matrices with unit diagonal are exactly Gram matrices of unit vectors in R^r, so Q_r is the ground-state energy of the r-component vector spin glass with a ferromagnetic term, and lambda_r^* is its ferromagnetic transition.
method: Identify q_r(lambda) with a known free energy, since the maximisation over rank-r psd matrices with unit diagonal is a spin system on the sphere.
obstruction: The vector-SK Parisi formula is a variational problem over monotone matrix paths rather than scalar paths, and its zero-temperature limit is not known in closed form for any r >= 2, so the reduction transfers the problem to another one that is open, albeit better studied. For r = 1 the answer follows from the Parisi formula for the SK model with ferromagnetic interaction; the source's question is exactly the r >= 2 case.
result: Writing X = sigma sigma^T with sigma_i in S^{r-1} (unit vectors in R^r), the constraint set is exactly the configuration space of the r-component vector spin model, and (1/n) Q_r is the ground-state energy of the r-vector Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model with an added ferromagnetic term of strength lambda. So q_r(lambda) is the zero-temperature limit of the vector-SK free energy with external ferromagnetic coupling, and lambda_r^* is the ferromagnetic-transition point of that model. This is not stated in the source and it converts the problem into one with an existing machinery: the Panisi-type variational formula for vector spin glasses (Panchenko) gives q_r(lambda) as a variational problem, and lambda_r^* is where the optimiser becomes non-trivial. The reduction is exact; the evaluation of the resulting variational problem at finite r is not carried out here.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For commuting diagonal A_k the norm is a maximum of d Gaussians and the (log d)^{1/2} is attained; for free-like A_k the norm is 2 sigma with no logarithm, so the conjecture asserts that the commuting case is extremal.
method: Check the conjecture against the two extreme cases that any candidate bound must reproduce, to see whether the exponent 1/2 is even the right guess.
obstruction: The two extremes are separated by the free-probability quantity that BBvH call intrinsic freeness, and the known interpolation loses a factor because the noncommutative moment method must control all moments simultaneously; the (log d)^{3/4} exponent in the literature comes from optimising a trace-moment bound of order p, and the gap to 1/2 is exactly the gap between a moment bound and a supremum bound over a net.
result: When the A_k commute and are diagonal, the norm is a maximum of d independent Gaussians with variances given by the rows, so E||X|| is of order sigma_* sqrt(log d) exactly, and sigma can be as small as sigma_*; the conjecture is TIGHT there, which is the source's reason for the exponent. At the opposite extreme, when the A_k are free-like (independent GUE-type), E||X|| tends to 2 sigma with no logarithm at all, so the conjecture is far from tight there but not violated. The conjecture therefore asserts that the commuting case is the worst, and that is a statement about interpolation between the two extremes. A caution about what a proof would NOT be: the trivial bound E||X|| <= sigma + sqrt(2 log d) times max_k ||A_k|| follows from a union bound over a net and is weaker than the conjecture whenever sigma_* is much smaller than max_k ||A_k||, so the conjecture is genuinely stronger than the union bound and any argument reproducing only the union bound is not progress.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Random signs give sqrt(n log n) by matrix Khintchine, and the rank-r restriction replaces the dimension n^2 by n r in that bound, which is exactly the room the known partial result uses.
method: Calibrate against the random signing and against the diagonal case, to see where the sqrt(n) must come from.
obstruction: Spencer's partial colouring lemma works in the cube with a body defined by n linear constraints; the matrix version needs a body defined by a spectral constraint, whose Gaussian measure is controlled only through the same matrix concentration inequality that carries the logarithm. The argument is therefore circular unless one has a logarithm-free spectral bound for a restricted class, which is what the rank restriction supplies.
result: Random signs give, by the matrix Chernoff/Khintchine bound, ||sum eps_k H_k|| of order sigma sqrt(log n) with sigma = ||sum H_k^2||^{1/2} <= sqrt(n), i.e. sqrt(n log n) - so exactly as in the scalar Spencer theorem, the random signing is off by sqrt(log n) and the conjecture asks for the partial-colouring gain. The rank restriction in the known result is not incidental: for rank-r matrices the effective dimension in the matrix Khintchine bound is n r rather than n^2, so the logarithm becomes log(nr) and the partial-colouring argument has room. The conjecture in full rank is therefore exactly the statement that the matrix Khintchine logarithm can be removed in the same way Spencer removed the scalar one - and by E0048 the logarithm in matrix Khintchine is itself not known to be improvable, so the two problems are linked: an affirmative answer to Open Problem 4.1 with the (log d)^{1/2} exponent would not by itself give matrix Spencer, but a bound with no logarithm at all would.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A k-lift of an n-vertex graph is an nk-dimensional object, so matrix Bernstein pays sqrt(log(nk)); the non-backtracking trace method pays nothing in k, so the two regimes together force a conjecture with no k-dependence.
method: Write down what each of the two known regimes gives and where they must meet.
obstruction: The trace method that gives Bordenave-Collins their result counts non-backtracking walks in the lift and is asymptotic in k with the base graph fixed; making it uniform in n requires controlling the number of walks in a growing base graph, where the combinatorial estimates degrade. Conversely matrix Bernstein cannot see the non-backtracking structure at all, which is where the logarithm is lost.
result: Oliveira's matrix-Bernstein bound gives sqrt(log(nk)) because the ambient dimension of the lift is nk; Bordenave-Collins give the dimension-free constant 2 sqrt(d-1) for fixed n and k tending to infinity. These two are compatible only if the logarithm in Oliveira's bound is an artefact of the dimension counting, and the natural conjecture the two regimes force is a bound of the form C sqrt(d) + o(1) uniformly in k, with the logarithm appearing only through n. That is: the correct conjecture is not 'more concentration for large k' but 'no k-dependence at all beyond the base graph's spectral data'. Stating the conjecture in that form, forced by matching the two regimes, is the useful output; no proof of uniformity is offered.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Markov gives only P(sum <= n+1) >= 1/(n+1), so the conjectured 1 - 1/e is not a restatement of the trivial bound; the extremal two-point law at 0 and n+1 attains 1 - (n/(n+1))^n, which decreases to 1 - 1/e.
method: Check the conjecture against the extremal example and against the trivial bound, since the campaign's own audit found a case where a 'result' turned out to be Markov's inequality in disguise.
obstruction: The difficulty is that the X_i need share no scale: some may be bounded and others heavy-tailed with the same mean, so no single truncation works, and the standard reduction to two-point laws (which is available for many such extremal problems by a Choquet argument) is blocked because the constraint set - independent, nonnegative, unit mean - is not compact in a topology making the objective continuous.
result: Markov gives P(sum > n+1) <= n/(n+1), i.e. P(sum <= n+1) >= 1/(n+1), which tends to 0 and is vastly weaker than 1 - 1/e - so the conjecture is genuinely more than the trivial bound, unlike the case the D-ledger audit caught. The extremal example is the two-point law at 0 and n+1, and it is worth noting that it is extremal in a strong sense: it puts the whole deviation into a single atom just above the threshold, so any proof must handle laws with an atom at exactly n+1 and cannot use any smoothness. A useful consequence of the extremal example: the conjecture cannot be improved to any constant larger than 1 - 1/e, and it is attained only in the limit, so the inequality should be strict for every finite n. That strictness is a checkable weaker statement.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Both extremal bisections equal d/4 plus or minus the same Parisi correction to leading order, so the conjecture is that the two sqrt(d) corrections cancel exactly, a symmetry statement rather than an evaluation.
method: Test the conjecture against the two regimes it must reconcile: large d, where the Parisi machinery applies, and small d, where it does not.
obstruction: The exact cancellation would follow from a sign symmetry exchanging the max-cut and min-cut problems, and no such symmetry exists on a fixed graph - it holds only in distribution and only to leading order, because the random regular graph is not bipartite and MinBis is bounded below by an odd-girth obstruction that has no MaxBis counterpart. Quantifying that asymmetry at fixed d is exactly the missing piece.
result: For large d the interpolation gives MaxBis/n = d/4 + P_* sqrt(d)/2 + o(sqrt(d)) and MinBis/n = d/4 - P_* sqrt(d)/2 + o(sqrt(d)) with P_* the Parisi constant, so the SUM is d/2 + o(sqrt(d)) automatically - the conjecture at large d is the statement that the two sqrt(d) corrections cancel EXACTLY, which the interpolation gives only to within o(sqrt(d)). So the conjecture's content at large d is an exact symmetry between the max and min problems, not a computation of either. At small d the interpolation is unavailable and the conjecture is a statement about the local structure of the random regular graph; the source itself points to Lyons's bounds as meaningful already at d = 3. Separating 'the corrections cancel' from 'the corrections are known' is the useful step: the conjecture is a symmetry claim.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The local weak limit of the sparse SBM is a Galton-Watson tree with a k-state symmetric broadcast, so the detection threshold IS the tree reconstruction threshold; Kesten-Stigum is the second-eigenvalue bound and is strictly loose for k >= 4.
method: State the two bounds that bracket the answer, and check whether the gap is an artefact or intrinsic.
obstruction: The tree reconstruction threshold for the symmetric k-state channel is known only through bounds (Mossel-Peres for the non-reconstruction side, Sly for k = 3, and asymptotics in k); an exact value for any k >= 4 is not known, and the non-reconstruction side requires a contraction estimate for the belief-propagation recursion that fails to be a simple second-moment computation once the Kesten-Stigum bound is not tight.
result: The Kesten-Stigum bound (a-b)^2 = k(a + (k-1)b) is the reconstruction threshold for the broadcast process on the Galton-Watson tree that describes the local limit, and it is exactly the point where the second eigenvalue of the broadcast kernel crosses the branching-number threshold. For k <= 3 tree reconstruction and Kesten-Stigum coincide; for k >= 4 they do not, and the local-limit correspondence shows the SBM detection threshold equals the TREE RECONSTRUCTION threshold, not Kesten-Stigum. So the question is not open as a graph question at all - it is exactly the open problem of determining the reconstruction threshold for the k-state symmetric channel on a Poisson tree, which is a cleaner and older problem. Saying that is the useful reduction: the source poses it as an SBM question and the mathematical content is entirely in the tree.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: With spectral initialisation the threshold is the BBP transition at sigma of order sqrt(n) and the projected power iteration only improves correlation; the genuinely open case is random initialisation, where the signal enters only at second order.
method: Separate the question into the two things a power-method analysis needs: a basin of attraction and an initialisation inside it.
obstruction: For random initialisation the first iterate is nearly orthogonal to z, so the signal appears only at second order and the analysis requires controlling the whole trajectory of a nonconvex iteration, for which the only available tool is a state-evolution argument that is proved for approximate message passing (with its Onsager correction) and not for the plain projected power method, whose iterates are correlated with the noise.
result: With spectral initialisation the analysis is essentially settled by the BBP transition: the top eigenvector of Y correlates with z as soon as sigma < sqrt(n), and one step of the projected power method improves the correlation monotonically, so the interesting regime is sigma of order sqrt(n) and the question is about constants, not orders. With RANDOM initialisation the picture is different: the iteration is then a nonconvex landscape question and the relevant threshold is where spurious local maxima of the likelihood disappear. So the source's single question is two questions with different answers, and the informative one is the random-initialisation case. That separation, and the observation that the spectral case reduces to BBP, is the useful step.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For x independent of W a union bound gives ||W x||_infinity of order sqrt(n log n), but the optimiser x^* is selected using W, and a union bound over all 2^n sign vectors would give only order n - the gap is the residual dependence of x^* on the noise.
method: Examine the sufficient condition the source names and test whether it can hold, since it involves the optimal solution rather than a fixed vector.
obstruction: Controlling the residual dependence requires a leave-one-out argument in which one coordinate of the noise is resampled and the maximiser is shown to move little - which is exactly the kind of stability that fails near the threshold, where the likelihood landscape has near-ties.
result: For a FIXED vector x independent of W, ||W x||_infinity is of order sqrt(n log n) by a union bound over n coordinates, so the sufficient condition is exactly what one would get if x^* were independent of the noise. The whole difficulty, and the reason the condition is not immediate, is that x^* is a function of W: it is the maximiser of x^T W x over the cube, so it is aligned with the noise, and the naive union bound does not apply. This is the same measurability obstruction as in E0033 (first-passage percolation geodesics). Quantifying it: the maximiser over 2^n sign vectors makes the effective union bound over 2^n vectors rather than n, which would give ||W x||_infinity of order n, not sqrt(n log n) - so a proof must exploit that x^* is close to z and hence nearly independent of W, and the residual dependence is what must be controlled.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The first two moments of multireference alignment observations do not identify the signal and the third (the bispectrum) does, which is why the sample complexity is of order sigma^6; the same degeneracy makes the Fisher information vanish and blocks the standard MLE consistency argument.
method: Ask what the sample-complexity answer implies about the estimator question, since the two are related but not equivalent.
obstruction: With a degenerate Fisher information the standard consistency proof (uniform law of large numbers plus a well-separated maximum) fails at the rate that matters: the likelihood surface is flat to second order along the directions the group action mixes, and controlling the empirical process on a flat surface requires uniform control at scale sigma^3, which is exactly the sample-complexity computation and not a corollary of it.
result: The sigma^6 rate comes from the third moment: the first two moments of the observations are invariant under the group action in a way that loses the phases, and the bispectrum (the third moment) is the first invariant that determines the signal, with estimation error of order sigma^3 / sqrt(n). Consistency of the MLE is a different claim: it asserts that maximising the likelihood, not the method of invariant moments, recovers the signal. The two agree only if the likelihood's population maximiser is unique up to the group, and the moment analysis shows precisely that the population second moment does NOT identify the signal - so the MLE's identifiability rests on the third-order behaviour of the likelihood at the true parameter, where the Fisher information degenerates. That degeneracy is the reason the question is nontrivial and the reason the sigma^6 rate is not sigma^2.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: phi_c(V(x)) - phi_c(x) = sum_i c_i log(1 + (Ax)_i) <= <c, Ax>, so sum_i c_i log x_i is a Lyapunov function exactly when c is a nonnegative vector with <c, Ax> <= 0 on the simplex, i.e. essentially when A^T c = 0.
method: Derive the whole family of Lyapunov functions of logarithmic type directly, and see what the source's question is asking one to leave.
obstruction: Any Lyapunov function must be nonincreasing on all trajectories, and the Volterra dynamics preserves the faces of the simplex, so a candidate must degenerate on every face; the log family is the only elementary family with that property. Beyond it one is looking for a function whose increment is controlled by a quadratic rather than a linear form in x, and the sign of a general quadratic form on the simplex is not decidable from skew-symmetry alone.
result: Take phi_c(x) = sum_i c_i log x_i with c_i >= 0. Along the Volterra map, phi_c(V(x)) - phi_c(x) = sum_i c_i log(1 + (Ax)_i), and since log(1+t) <= t this is at most <c, Ax> for every x in the simplex. So phi_c is nonincreasing along every trajectory as soon as <c, Ax> <= 0 for all x in the simplex, and in particular whenever A^T c = 0, in which case the bound is exactly 0 and phi_c decreases strictly unless (Ax)_i = 0 for every i with c_i > 0. This identifies the known Lyapunov family precisely as the nonnegative kernel of A^T, and shows the construction is exhausted by that kernel - which is why the source asks for another KIND. The concrete consequence: for a skew-symmetric A of full rank on the relevant subspace there is no such c at all, so those operators have no logarithmic Lyapunov function and are exactly where a new one is needed. A caution: this derivation is elementary and is presumably known to the authors; it is recorded because it delimits the search.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Odd-order principal minors of a skew-symmetric matrix vanish identically, which is why the Volterra transversality condition mentions only even orders; the intrinsic statement is that 0 is a regular value of V - id on every face.
method: Ask what transversality is FOR, since the definition should be chosen so that the theorem it supports survives. In the Volterra case its consequence is finiteness of the fixed-point set.
obstruction: For a non-Volterra QSO the fixed-point equation is genuinely quadratic and its solution set is a variety rather than a linear subspace, so 'regular value' is a condition on P AND on the fixed point, not on P alone; a necessary and sufficient condition purely in terms of P would have to be an elimination-theoretic statement (a discriminant of the quadratic system), which exists in principle but is not a usable criterion for m >= 4.
result: Finiteness of the fixed point set is exactly transversality of the map x -> V(x) - x to zero, i.e. that 0 is a regular value of V - id on each face of the simplex. That is the definition that generalises, and it is intrinsic: it does not mention minors. For a Volterra QSO it specialises correctly because there V(x) - x = (x_i (Ax)_i)_i, whose zero set on the interior of a face is the solution set of a linear system with matrix a principal submatrix of A, and regularity of that system on all faces is precisely non-vanishing of the even-order principal minors (odd-order principal minors of a skew-symmetric matrix vanish automatically, which is why only even orders appear). So the source's minor condition is the Volterra shadow of 'zero is a regular value', and the general definition should be the latter. The remaining work - translating regularity into conditions on P - is a determinantal condition on the derivative DV(x) - I along the fixed-point set, which is not a condition on P alone.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A periodic itinerary is a trajectory shadowing a heteroclinic cycle among the fixed points; its existence is governed by the product of contraction-to-expansion eigenvalue ratios around the cycle, not by the existence of a periodic orbit.
method: Recognise the object: a trajectory spending almost all its time near a finite set of saddles and moving between them is shadowing a heteroclinic network, and its itinerary is the sequence of nodes visited in that network.
obstruction: Shadowing a heteroclinic cycle for infinite time requires the cycle to be asymptotically stable, and stability of a heteroclinic cycle depends on the ratio of eigenvalues around it exceeding one; for a skew-symmetric A those ratios are constrained but not obviously on the right side, and no criterion in terms of A is known. If the cycle is unstable, generic trajectories eventually leave and the itinerary is aperiodic.
result: A periodic itinerary is therefore a trajectory shadowing a heteroclinic CYCLE in the network whose nodes are the fixed points and whose edges are the connecting orbits. Two consequences follow immediately. First, existence requires the network to contain a cycle at all, which is a purely combinatorial condition on the signs of the eigenvalues of DV at each fixed point - checkable from A. Second, even when a cycle exists, the residence times near successive saddles grow geometrically with ratio the product of the ratios of contracting to expanding eigenvalues around the cycle, so the itinerary is periodic while the timing is not; the source's question is about the itinerary alone, which is exactly the shadowing statement and not an asymptotic-stability statement. Making that distinction is the useful step: one is asked for a periodic SYMBOL sequence, not a periodic orbit, and periodic orbits are typically absent while periodic itineraries need not be.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: All three parameters of the same sign makes the tournament cyclic and the interior fixed point a repeller, which is Zakharevich's failure mechanism; mixed signs make the tournament transitive and the dynamics gradient-like.
method: Identify the mechanism behind the failure in the known case and ask whether its negation is the right dividing line.
obstruction: Gradient-like behaviour gives convergence of trajectories to the fixed-point set but not convergence of Cesaro averages when the omega-limit set is a continuum, and a Volterra QSO with a degenerate a_{ij} can have a segment of fixed points. Ruling that out needs the transversality of Problem 2, which is itself unresolved for these operators.
result: When a, b, c share a sign the three-species system is a cyclic (rock-paper-scissors) competition and the interior fixed point is a repeller, so trajectories spiral outward to the boundary heteroclinic cycle; the Cesaro averages then oscillate between the three vertices without converging, which is exactly Zakharevich's mechanism. If the signs are NOT all equal the cycle is broken - one of the three pairwise comparisons is reversed - so there is a transitive ordering on the three types and the dynamics is gradient-like, which is the situation in which Cesaro convergence should hold. So the source's dividing line is the presence or absence of a cyclic tournament, and the conjecture that its absence suffices is structurally plausible. What is missing, and it is not a technicality: the degenerate cases where one of a, b, c is zero leave a two-dimensional invariant face on which the argument must be run separately, and the source's condition excludes zeros only in the failure direction.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The sign pattern of the skew-symmetric A is a tournament and V is the discrete replicator map for it; in continuous time the Cesaro limit exists and equals the interior equilibrium whenever one exists, so the natural criterion is existence of an interior optimal strategy of the tournament game.
method: Use the tournament reading of E0061 and ask what the right generalisation of 'all signs equal' is for m > 3.
obstruction: The replicator time-average theorem is a continuous-time statement whose proof integrates d(log x_i)/dt; the discrete map replaces that derivative by log(1 + (Ax)_i), which differs from (Ax)_i at second order, and the accumulated second-order error over n steps is exactly of the same order as the quantity being averaged. Zakharevich's counterexample shows the error is not negligible.
result: The sign pattern of a skew-symmetric A is a tournament on m vertices, and the Volterra dynamics on the simplex is the discrete-time analogue of the replicator dynamics for that tournament. For replicator dynamics the classical dichotomy is between tournaments that admit an interior evolutionarily stable point (the matrix game has an interior optimal strategy, equivalently the tournament has a Nash equilibrium with full support) and those that do not; the former have convergent time averages by the standard replicator time-average theorem, which says that if trajectories stay in a compact subset of the interior then the Cesaro limit is the interior equilibrium. So the natural conjecture, which the source does not state, is: the ergodic theorem holds for a Volterra QSO if and only if the associated tournament game has an interior optimal strategy, and it fails exactly when the game's optimal strategies live on a proper face. The m = 3 case of that conjecture is exactly Theorem 3 and Problem 4. This is a proposed criterion, not a theorem: the discrete-time replicator map does not obey the continuous-time time-average theorem, and that is where the work would be.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For any partition into q blocks, Cauchy-Schwarz gives sum_p (sum_{i in E_p} x_i)^2 >= 1/q, so a pi-QSO puts mass at least 1/q on the empty body at every step - a uniform bound that does not depend on q's structure.
method: Test the q = 2 proof against q >= 3 by tracking why the 'empty body' state absorbs.
obstruction: The definition of a pi-QSO constrains only same-block pairs; cross-block pairs may have arbitrary P_{ij,k}, so the mass produced at states other than 0 is uncontrolled and can be recycled into cross-block pairs at the next step. Whether that recycling can sustain a nontrivial fixed point is exactly what the Cauchy-Schwarz bound does not decide.
result: With two classes, any pair from the same class produces only the empty body 0, and reproduction requires one member of each class, so the mass at 0 is non-decreasing along the trajectory and strictly increases unless the population is concentrated in one class - which is why (1,0,...,0) is the unique fixed point and the convergence is exponential. With q >= 3 blocks the same monotonicity STILL holds, because P_{ij,k} = 0 for i and j in the same block forces those pairs to contribute to 0 as well, so x_0' >= sum_p (sum_{i in E_p} x_i)^2 >= 1/q by Cauchy-Schwarz. That gives an immediate quantitative statement the source does not record: for any pi-QSO the mass at the empty body satisfies x_0(n+1) >= 1/q, hence the trajectory enters and stays in the region {x_0 >= 1/q} after one step, and the convergence to (1,0,...,0) then follows from x_0' >= x_0^2 + 1/q(1-x_0)^2 whenever the cross terms cannot escape 0. This is a proof sketch of the analogue under the stated hypothesis and should be checked; the Cauchy-Schwarz step is exact but the last inequality assumes the cross-block coefficients sum to at most 1, which the definition permits but does not force.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Strict non-Volterra means P_{ij,k} = 0 for k in {i,j}, so DV has zero diagonal and zero trace everywhere; Euler's identity for a homogeneous quadratic map gives DV(x*) x* = 2 x*, so the m-1 tangential eigenvalues sum to -2 and one of them has modulus at least 2/(m-1) - which exceeds 1 only when m <= 3.
method: Ask which half of Theorem 6 is a counting statement and which is a stability statement, since they have different m-dependence.
obstruction: The bound 2/(m-1) is only a bound, so it does not construct an attracting example; producing one requires choosing P with all eigenvalues of DV inside the unit disc subject to zero diagonal and row sums 2, which is a feasibility problem that grows with m and has not been solved here.
result: Uniqueness of the fixed point is a Brouwer-plus-degree statement: V maps the simplex to itself continuously, so at least one fixed point exists for every m, and uniqueness asserts that the degree computation has no cancellation. Non-attractiveness is a spectral statement, and here the strict non-Volterra structure gives something usable in every dimension. Since P_{ij,k} = 0 whenever k is in {i,j}, the diagonal of the derivative vanishes identically: dV_k/dx_k = 2 sum_j P_{kj,k} x_j = 0, so trace DV(x) = 0 at every point. On the other hand V is homogeneous of degree 2, so Euler's identity gives DV(x*) x* = 2 V(x*) = 2 x* at a fixed point: 2 is always an eigenvalue, with the radial direction as eigenvector. Since the trace is zero, the remaining m-1 eigenvalues - the ones acting on the tangent space of the simplex, which are what decides attractiveness - sum to -2, so at least one of them has modulus at least 2/(m-1). For m = 3 that lower bound is 1, which reproduces Theorem 6's non-attractiveness; for m >= 4 it drops below 1 and the argument no longer excludes an attracting fixed point. That is a concrete reason to expect Theorem 6 to FAIL for large m, and it is not in the source.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: At m = 2 the general bound 1/(2m) = 0.25 exceeds the exact lambda_2 = (3 - sqrt(7))/2 = 0.177 by about 41 per cent, which calibrates the expected size of lambda_m as roughly (3 - sqrt(7))/m rather than 1/(2m).
method: Check the two given data points against each other, since they are stated for the same quantity and should be consistent.
obstruction: The exact m = 2 value comes from solving a one-dimensional dynamical problem explicitly (the simplex is an interval), and for m >= 3 the extremal operator realising the threshold is not known even conjecturally; the threshold is an infimum over a semialgebraic set of operators, so exact values will be algebraic numbers of growing degree and there is no reason for a closed form.
result: They are consistent but only just, and the comparison is informative. At m = 2 the general bound gives lambda_2 <= 1/4 = 0.25, while the exact value is (3 - sqrt(7))/2 = 0.17712..., so the general bound overshoots by about 41 per cent at the only point where both are known. Since the constraint sum_k P_{ij,k} = 1 forces P_{ij,k} <= 1 - (m-1) lambda for the threshold to be attainable at all, the admissible range of lambda_m shrinks like 1/m, and the exact value should behave like c/m for some constant c strictly below 1/2. The m = 2 datum suggests c is near 2 lambda_2 = 3 - sqrt(7) = 0.354, i.e. lambda_m of order 0.354/m rather than 0.5/m. That is a prediction with one data point behind it and should be treated as such - it is an extrapolation, not a derivation.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Bistochasticity means V(x) is majorised by x, so every Schur-concave function - in particular the Shannon entropy - is nondecreasing along trajectories, and the omega-limit set lies in the entropy-preserving set.
method: Use majorisation directly: bistochasticity says V(x) is majorised by x, so every Schur-concave function increases along trajectories.
obstruction: The entropy-preserving set can be large. For the identity-like extreme points of the bistochastic set, every point preserves entropy and nothing is learned; conversely for operators with a strict majorisation the set is the centre of the simplex. Deciding which case a given P is in requires the classification of extreme quadratic bistochastic operators, which is known only for small m.
result: That gives the dynamics a Lyapunov function for free, and a canonical one: the Shannon entropy H(x) = -sum_i x_i log x_i is Schur-concave, so H(V(x)) >= H(x) for every bistochastic V and every x. Hence H is nondecreasing along every trajectory and bounded above by log m, so H(x(n)) converges; the omega-limit set of any trajectory is therefore contained in a level set of H, and any limit point y satisfies H(V(y)) = H(y), i.e. lies in the set where the entropy is exactly preserved. That is a genuine structural answer to the source's question, and it is elementary: the trajectories of a quadratic bistochastic operator are entropy-monotone and accumulate on the entropy-preserving set. In particular, if the only entropy-preserving points are the permutations of a fixed vector, every trajectory converges to that orbit. What this does not do: identify the entropy-preserving set for a given V, which is where the real classification work is.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For the fully cyclic Volterra QSO on S^2 the interior fixed point is a repeller and every interior trajectory approaches the boundary heteroclinic cycle, so the historic set is the entire interior and has full measure.
method: Use the m = 3 counterexample of Zakharevich as a seed and ask whether its historic set has positive measure.
obstruction: Producing coexistence requires an operator whose simplex splits into two basins, one of which is a stable heteroclinic cycle. For Volterra operators the boundary cycle is either attracting for all interior points or repelling, by the sign structure of A, so coexistence needs a non-Volterra operator, where no Lyapunov theory is available at all.
result: In Zakharevich's example (a = b = c = 1, the fully cyclic Volterra operator on S^2) the interior fixed point is a repeller and every interior trajectory spirals out to the boundary heteroclinic cycle, so the Cesaro averages oscillate for EVERY interior initial condition - the historic set is the whole interior, which has full measure in the simplex. So a class with the required property already exists in the source's own text, and the question's content must be the case where the historic set is neither null nor everything, or where the operator is not Volterra. Recording that the fully cyclic Volterra operator answers the literal question is the honest reading; if the intended question is a nondegenerate one (historic behaviour coexisting with a positive-measure set of convergent trajectories) then the target is a QSO with two attractors, one a heteroclinic cycle and one a fixed point.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: V^r = V means V restricted to its image W is a bijection of order dividing r-1; since a genuinely quadratic map has degree 2^{r-1} on iterates, finite order forces W to be degenerate or V to be affine on W.
method: Translate V^r = V into a statement about the image and the dynamics on it, before any algebra.
obstruction: A quadratic map cannot have finite order on a set with nonempty interior unless it is affine there, because the degree of V^{r-1} is 2^{r-1} and equals 1 only if cancellation is total; so either W has empty interior in the simplex, or V is affine on W. Deciding which of these occurs for a given P is the classification, and it requires the elimination theory that made the Bernstein problem hard already at r = 2.
result: V^r = V says that V restricted to its own image W = V(S^{m-1}) satisfies V^{r-1} = id on W, so V|_W is a bijection of finite order r-1. Hence the classification splits into two independent parts: (i) the structure of the image W and the retraction of the simplex onto it, and (ii) the finite-order group generated by V|_W, which is a cyclic group of order dividing r-1 acting on W. The Bernstein case r = 2 is exactly the case where that group is trivial, which is why it is a pure algebra problem (idempotents of the Bernstein algebra). For r >= 3 the new content is a finite cyclic symmetry of W realised by a quadratic map, and since W is a compact convex-image subset of the simplex and V|_W is a homeomorphism of finite order, Brouwer gives a fixed point of V|_W and the action linearises near it up to conjugacy. That decomposition - retraction plus finite cyclic action - is the shape of the answer and is not stated in the source.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For symmetric mu the left and right Poisson boundaries agree and every bounded harmonic function is bi-harmonic, so the question has content only for non-symmetric measures.
method: Compare the two one-sided problems, since a bi-harmonic function must be harmonic for both the left and the right walk.
obstruction: For non-symmetric mu the left and right Poisson boundaries are different measure spaces with no canonical map between them, so a common nonconstant function need not exist; constructing one requires a coupling of the two boundaries, and the only natural candidate - the double boundary of the bilateral walk - carries no invariant function by the Kaimanovich double-boundary argument.
result: A left mu-harmonic function is a limit of boundary data on the Poisson boundary (B, nu) of (G, mu) and a right mu-harmonic function corresponds to the boundary of the reflected measure mu-check. A bi-harmonic function is therefore a function measurable with respect to both boundaries at once, i.e. a joint invariant, and the question becomes whether the two boundary sigma-algebras have a nontrivial common refinement realised inside the space of bounded functions on G. This makes the answer immediate in one important case: for a SYMMETRIC mu the two boundaries coincide, so every nonconstant bounded harmonic function is bi-harmonic, and the question is nontrivial only for non-symmetric mu, where the two boundaries can be genuinely different. Restricting to non-symmetric measures is the useful reduction and the source does not state it.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The induced walk on G/H is still G-equivariant, so the entropy criterion applies with the conditional entropy given the coset; a wreath product with H the finitary base subgroup has infinite index and an amenable Liouville quotient walk.
method: Ask what the Liouville property means on a coset space and where the standard proofs of it use the group structure.
obstruction: Quasi-harmonic functions are only asymptotically harmonic, so triviality of the Poisson boundary does not exclude them; the source's question deliberately asks for the stronger conclusion. Excluding quasi-harmonic functions needs a statement about the tail rather than the invariant sigma-algebra, and tail-triviality of the coset walk does not follow from tail-triviality of the walk on G.
result: On a group, the Liouville property is equivalent to triviality of the Poisson boundary and is proved via the entropy criterion (the Avez entropy of mu vanishes) or via amenability plus a Folner argument. Both proofs use the transitive action of G on itself by translations. On G/H the walk is still G-equivariant, so the entropy criterion survives in the form: the boundary of the induced walk on G/H is trivial if the conditional entropy of the position given the coset vanishes. So a construction should aim at a pair (G, H) with H so large - though of infinite index - that the coset walk is recurrent or has zero conditional entropy. The natural candidate family is G a wreath product and H the subgroup of finitely supported configurations, where the coset space is the base group and the induced walk is the projection, which is a random walk on an amenable group with the Liouville property. That candidate makes 'infinite index' and 'Liouville quotient' compatible; whether it also kills QUASI-harmonic functions, which are weaker, is the residual point.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Guivarch's fundamental inequality (speed times growth exponent at most entropy) turns triviality of the projected Poisson boundary into zero speed whenever the quotient has exponential growth, leaving only subexponential-growth metrics.
method: Interpret the conclusion as sublinear drift and ask what ergodicity of H on the boundary buys.
obstruction: The fundamental inequality is proved for random walks on groups, and its coset-space version requires an entropy for a non-transitive action; if the metric d has subexponential growth the inequality is vacuous even on groups, and the source's problem allows any invariant metric.
result: The quantity is the Cesaro average of the expected distance from the origin coset, so the assertion is that the walk projected to G/H has zero SPEED in the Cesaro sense. Ergodicity of H on the boundary says that the boundary carries no nonconstant H-invariant function, which is exactly the statement that the projected walk has trivial Poisson boundary - and for a walk with trivial boundary the entropy vanishes, hence by the fundamental inequality (Guivarch) speed times the growth exponent is at most entropy, so the speed vanishes whenever the growth of (G/H, d) is exponential. That is a genuine derivation of the conjecture in the exponential-growth case, and it isolates the remaining case: metrics of subexponential growth on G/H, where the fundamental inequality gives nothing. The derivation uses the standard fundamental inequality for coset spaces, which I have not verified in the literature in that generality, so the claim is conditional on that transfer.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: A conjugation-invariant semi-metric gives a class function, and for a symmetric walk each homogeneous quasi-morphism has zero drift by inversion symmetry; Bavard duality expresses stable commutator length as a supremum of such quasi-morphisms, so the conjecture is an interchange of supremum and limit.
method: Use symmetry of mu together with conjugation invariance of d, which are the only two hypotheses, and see what they force.
obstruction: The supremum in Bavard duality is over an infinite-dimensional set of quasi-morphisms with unbounded defect, and the drift of the supremum can exceed the supremum of the drifts; controlling the interchange needs a uniform bound on the defects that is not available in the commutator subgroup of the free group.
result: Conjugation invariance means d(g,h) depends only on the conjugacy class of g^{-1} h, so the function g -> d(e,g) is a class function; symmetry of mu means the walk is reversible. The drift is then the limit of (1/n) E[phi(X_n)] for a class function phi that is subadditive along the walk. Subadditivity plus symmetry gives one immediate consequence: the walk is reversible, so E[phi(X_n)] is nondecreasing and the limit exists, and it vanishes if and only if phi(X_n) = o(n) in expectation. The special structure available here is that a conjugation-invariant semi-metric is a quasi-morphism-type object - by Bavard duality, the stable commutator length is the supremum of homogeneous quasi-morphisms - and for a SYMMETRIC walk every homogeneous quasi-morphism has zero drift, because phi(X_n)/n converges to a translation number which must be symmetric under inversion and hence zero. That reduces the conjecture, in the stable-commutator-length case the source names, to interchanging the supremum over quasi-morphisms with the limit in n. That interchange is the whole difficulty and is not justified here.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: In the measure-preserving case non-ergodicity of the self-product produces eigenfunctions and hence a Kronecker factor; over the Poisson boundary the action is stationary, not measure preserving, so the invariant function is only stationary and the spectral argument has no starting point.
method: Recognise the shape: non-ergodicity of the self-product is the classical signal of a nontrivial Kronecker factor, so the question asks for a relative Furstenberg-Zimmer dichotomy over the Poisson boundary.
obstruction: Stationary actions have no unitary representation of G on L^2 preserving the measure, so the eigenfunction argument has no starting point; the substitutes (Nevo-Zimmer structure theory) apply to higher-rank semisimple groups and not to a general measured group.
result: In the measure-preserving setting the implication is a theorem: an ergodic system whose self-product is non-ergodic has a nontrivial Kronecker (isometric) factor, obtained from the eigenfunctions witnessing the non-ergodic invariant function. The obstruction to importing it is precisely that a (G, mu)-space over the Poisson boundary is NOT measure preserving - the boundary is only stationary - so the invariant function on X x X produced by non-ergodicity is stationary rather than invariant, and there is no spectral theorem for stationary actions to produce eigenfunctions from it. Naming that as the single missing ingredient (a spectral theory for stationary actions, which is what the Furstenberg-Glasner theory of stationary joinings supplies only partially) is the useful step.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Gated service is of branching type and one-limited is not, so the mixed system leaves Resing's multitype branching framework; the resulting kernel is branching in one variable and linear in the other and is not a genus-zero algebraic curve.
method: Classify the functional equation, since the analytic method that applies is determined by whether the underlying branching structure is a multitype branching process with immigration.
obstruction: The boundary value method needs the kernel to define a Riemann surface of genus zero or one; with a gated component the kernel is not polynomial of degree two in each variable (the branching component contributes a composition rather than a product), so the surface is not defined and the Tutte-invariant or Riemann-Hilbert machinery does not start.
result: Gated service is of branching type (each customer present at the polling instant is replaced during the visit by the customers arriving during its service), while one-limited service is not: exactly one customer is served regardless of the queue length, so the offspring generating function is degenerate. The mixed system therefore falls outside Resing's branching-type framework, which is precisely why the standard product-form solution fails, and the iteration the source describes is the symptom. What the equation IS is a two-variable functional equation with a kernel that is linear in one variable and of branching type in the other - the same class as the Fayolle-Iasnogorodski random walk in the quarter plane with one reflecting and one branching boundary. That identification points to the boundary-value method as the right tool and predicts a solution expressible through a conformal gluing function rather than in closed form, which is consistent with the source's failed attempts at an explicit answer.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: For large deterministic switch-over time S the arrivals per cycle satisfy a law of large numbers by Blackwell's renewal theorem for any renewal input; the Poisson-specific input is only the independence of successive cycles, which for renewal arrivals is carried by the residual interarrival time at the polling epochs.
method: Ask what the limit statement is really saying, so as to identify the minimal probabilistic input.
obstruction: Tightness of the residual life uniformly in S fails for heavy-tailed interarrival distributions with infinite mean residual life, so the conjecture as stated needs a moment condition that the source does not impose; with a finite second moment the reduction should be completable, and the general renewal case may simply be false.
result: As the deterministic switch-over time S grows, each cycle lasts at least the total switch-over time, so the number of arrivals per cycle at queue i is A_i(S(1+o(1))), and the assertion that the system becomes deterministic is exactly a law of large numbers for the renewal counting process over a long cycle, plus the statement that the fluctuations do not accumulate across cycles. The first part is free for ANY renewal process with finite mean - that is Blackwell's theorem, not a branching argument - so the Poisson-specific machinery is not needed for the leading order. What the branching argument supplies in the Poisson case, and what is genuinely missing in general, is the second part: uniform control of the correlation between successive cycle lengths, which for a renewal process involves the residual interarrival time carried across the polling instant. So the conjecture reduces to showing that the residual-life process at the polling epochs is tight uniformly in S, which is a statement about the renewal process alone and does not involve the polling discipline. That reduction is the useful output.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The large switch-over limit needs only a law of large numbers for arrivals over a long cycle plus asymptotic decoupling of cycles, so the natural classifying condition is that the work left behind at each visit is o(S) - satisfied by exhaustive and gated service and violated by k-limited service.
method: Ask what property of a discipline the limit theorem actually uses, given the reduction in E0075.
obstruction: For dynamic visit orders the sequence of visited queues is itself random and depends on the state, so 'cycle' is not well defined and the decoupling in (ii) has to be proved for a Markov-modulated sequence of visits; the natural regeneration structure (returning to a fixed queue with an empty system) may have infinite expected length under a greedy dynamic policy.
result: The reduction there shows the limit needs only (i) a law of large numbers for arrivals over a long cycle and (ii) asymptotic decoupling of successive cycles. Neither mentions the visit order, so a discipline should exhibit the behaviour whenever the SERVICE rule leaves a bounded amount of work carried across a polling instant relative to the switch-over time. That gives a candidate classification: the deterministic limit holds for every discipline in which the work left behind at a queue after its visit is o(S) in probability - which includes exhaustive and gated service (work left behind is zero or the arrivals during the visit) and excludes k-limited service with fixed k, where the work left behind grows linearly with the cycle length. This is a proposed criterion consistent with the known Poisson results and with the source's simulations; it is not proved, and in particular the k-limited exclusion should be checked against the numerics before it is believed.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: c^2 >= 1 is equivalent to nonnegativity of pi D D_Q^# D 1, a quadratic form in the deviation matrix; for a reversible modulating chain that matrix is self-adjoint and positive semidefinite off the constants, so the conjecture holds there and only the non-reversible case is open.
method: Test the conjecture on the structure the source gives: c^2 = d_2 - 1 where d_2 = 1 + 2 pi D D_Q^# D 1 in their notation, so the claim is a sign statement about a deviation-matrix quadratic form.
obstruction: For a non-reversible generator the deviation matrix has complex spectrum and its symmetric part need not be positive semidefinite, so the quadratic form can in principle be negative; whether the specific vectors appearing (the arrival-rate diagonal D applied to the stationary vector) can realise a negative value is the residual question, and it is a finite-dimensional but unbounded-dimension optimisation.
result: The conjecture is equivalent to the nonnegativity of a quadratic form built from the deviation matrix D_Q^# = integral over u >= 0 of (e^{Qu} - 1 pi) du of the modulating chain. That form is not a Gram matrix in general - the deviation matrix of a non-reversible chain is not symmetric - which is exactly why the folklore proof does not exist. For a REVERSIBLE modulating chain the deviation matrix is self-adjoint in the stationary inner product with nonnegative spectrum on the orthogonal complement of the constants, so the quadratic form is nonnegative and c^2 >= 1 follows. That gives the conjecture for all reversible MMPPs, which includes every two-state MMPP (all two-state chains are reversible) - and the source's own non-monotone hazard-rate counterexample is a four-state chain with a cyclic Q, i.e. non-reversible. So the honest statement is: the conjecture holds for reversible modulating chains, and the open case is exactly the non-reversible one. This should be checked against the source's exact normalisation of D_Q^# before being quoted.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Usual stochastic dominance between two variables with the same mean forces equality in law, so the intended relation must be the convex order; a mixture of exponentials always dominates the matched exponential in convex order by Jensen, and the gap is exactly the chain's motion within an inter-event interval.
method: Relate the two conjectures, since a stochastic ordering is stronger than a moment inequality and the source presents them together.
obstruction: When the modulating chain jumps during an inter-event interval the law of T is a phase-type distribution rather than a mixture of exponentials, and phase-type laws are not automatically above the exponential in the convex order - the source's own four-state example with a non-monotone hazard rate shows the failure of the simplest sufficient condition (decreasing hazard rate).
result: Conjecture 4.2 implies Conjecture 4.1 only if the ordering is in the convex order, not the usual stochastic order: usual stochastic dominance between two variables with the SAME mean forces them to be equal in law, so if the two variables in the source's statement have equal means the intended relation must be convex or dilation order, under which the variance inequality c^2 >= 1 is immediate. That is worth flagging as a reading issue in the source's statement rather than a mathematical obstacle. Under the convex-order reading, the natural proof route is a mixture representation: conditionally on the modulating chain's stationary sojourn structure the inter-event time is exponential with a state-dependent rate, and a MIXTURE of exponentials is always larger in the convex order than the exponential with the same mean - by Jensen applied to the convex function t -> E[exp(-lambda t)]. That argument works whenever the inter-event time is a genuine mixture of exponentials, which is the case when the modulating chain does not move during an inter-event interval; the general MMPP allows the chain to move, and that is exactly the gap.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: t -> (B_{t+u} - B_t; 0 <= u <= 1) is a stationary Markov process on C[0,1] with Wiener stationary law, so scannability of S is a capacity statement, not a measure statement - which is why measure-zero pattern sets can still occur.
method: Recognise the structure: the map t -> theta_t B, the shifted and recentred path, is a stationary Markov process on C[0,1] with the Wiener measure as its stationary law, so the question is whether S is hit by a stationary process.
obstruction: The shift process on Wiener space is not symmetric, so no Dirichlet form is available to compute the capacity, which is precisely the source's own Open problem 4.2. Without a Dirichlet form the only tool is a direct first- and second-moment estimate on the discrete-time analogue, which the source carries out for a few explicit families.
result: For a stationary process the hitting question is governed by a capacity, not a measure, which is exactly why S can have Wiener measure zero and still be scannable - the source's own examples (excursions, first-passage bridges) all have measure zero. Two immediate consequences that delimit the answer: (i) if S is open and nonempty then S is scannable, because the shifted process has full support and is recurrent; (ii) if S is closed with empty interior, scannability depends on the capacity that the source later introduces as CapMW, and the source's own non-existence theorem for the normalised excursion shows that some natural closed sets are not scannable. So the classification asked for is a capacity-zero criterion for the shift process on Wiener space, which is the content of the source's Question 1.5-prime, and the honest reading is that Question 1.5 as posed is not a separate problem but the qualitative form of that capacity question.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Positive Wiener measure implies positive CapMW by stationarity at T = 0, so the shift capacity dominates the measure; the whole classification problem lives on the measure-zero sets.
method: Compare CapMW with the classical Wiener-space capacities to see which tools transfer.
obstruction: Choquet capacitability gives measurability of the hitting probability but no computation. Computing CapMW for a specific S' requires a second-moment estimate on the set of times t with theta_t B in S', and for pattern sets defined by path constraints the correlation between two such times decays only polynomially, so the second-moment method is critical rather than convergent.
result: CapMW is the hitting capacity of a stationary, non-symmetric Markov process, whereas the Malliavin-Fukushima capacity CapX on Wiener space is the capacity of a SYMMETRIC Dirichlet form (the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck form). The two are therefore capacities of different processes on the same space, and there is no a priori inequality between them - the source's Open problem 4.2 asks exactly for a relation. What can be said without any theory is a one-sided comparison at the level of null sets: any set of positive Wiener measure has positive CapMW (take T = 0 and use stationarity), so CapMW dominates the measure; and any set that is polar for the OU process still may be hit by the shift. So the useful classification target is the intermediate class of measure-zero sets, and the shift capacity is strictly finer than the measure. This is a delimitation, not a criterion.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Conway's system sum_w pi_w C(w,v) = E T(A) for all v in A determines E T(A) exactly from the pairwise correlation polynomials, so the asymptotics of E T(A_n) is a spectral question about the correlation matrix of the family, not a counting question.
method: Use the martingale (Conway leading number) identity for a collection, which is exact for any finite A_n, and read off what the asymptotics needs.
obstruction: The linear system has |A_n| unknowns, which grows exponentially, and its matrix of pairwise correlations has no product structure for the natural families (excursions, bridges, first passage), so the asymptotics requires a spectral estimate on an exponentially large correlation matrix rather than a combinatorial count.
result: For a collection A of patterns in a fair coin sequence, the gambling-team martingale gives the exact relation sum over patterns w in A of P(the pattern seen is w) times the correlation polynomial of w with itself equals E T(A) - more precisely E T(A) = sum_w pi_w C(w,w) where C is the autocorrelation value and pi_w the probability that w occurs first, together with the consistency relations sum_w pi_w C(w,v) = E T(A) for every v in A. So the exact answer is a finite linear system whose data are the pairwise correlation polynomials, and the asymptotics in n is entirely a question about the CORRELATION STRUCTURE of the family A_n, not about its size. That explains the source's own examples: discrete excursions of length 2n have E T of order n^{3/2} while there are of order 4^n / n^{3/2} of them, so the naive count |A_n|^{-1} 2^n is off by a factor n^{3} - the discrepancy is exactly the correlation. Naming the linear system as the object to analyse is the useful step.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Discrete excursions of length 2n number about 4^n n^{-3/2} and bridges about 4^n n^{-1/2}, matching the observed waiting-time exponents 3/2 and 1; the missing exact constants are the correlation corrections in Conway's system.
method: Ask what upgrading two-sided bounds to exact asymptotics needs in this framework.
obstruction: The set of self-overlaps of a bridge pattern depends on the pattern, not just on n, so the correlation correction is an average over the family with respect to the unknown weights pi_w, and those weights are exactly what the system determines - the computation is circular unless one shows pi_w is asymptotically uniform.
result: By the correlation-system identity of E0081, an exact constant requires the limit of the normalised solution of the Conway system, i.e. the limit of the empirical distribution pi_w over the family together with the limiting correlation profile. For the excursion family the source obtains the exponent 3/2 from the Catalan count k(E_{2n}) of order 4^n n^{-3/2}, so the exact constant there is the ratio of that count to 2^{2n} times a correlation correction. For bridges the count is the central binomial coefficient, of order 4^n n^{-1/2}, so the scaling-limit exponent 1 is consistent, and the missing constant is precisely the correlation correction - which for bridges should be computable because a bridge's autocorrelation is supported on the shifts that preserve the endpoint constraint, a set of size of order sqrt(n). That gives a concrete prediction that the correction is a constant rather than a power, so the answer should be E T(BR_{alpha,n}) asymptotic to c(alpha) n with c(alpha) an explicit theta-like constant. This is a prediction from the counting plus correlation structure, not a computation.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The set of paths whose maximum is attained at time zero is hit by the shift at every record time of B, hence has positive CapMW, while being Malliavin-polar; so no domination of CapMW by CapX can hold.
method: Compare the null sets of the two capacities on the source's own examples, since a relation must at least be consistent with those.
obstruction: A relation in the other direction would need CapX to dominate CapMW, and there is no reason for it: CapX measures sensitivity to perturbations in Cameron-Martin directions, CapMW measures hitting by a time shift, and the two directions of variation are not comparable - the shift is not absolutely continuous with respect to the Cameron-Martin translations.
result: The two capacities cannot be equivalent. The set of paths of finite quadratic variation different from t, for instance, is CapX-polar (it is a set of Malliavin capacity zero, being excluded by the OU quasi-sure quadratic variation theorem) but is hit by the shift with probability zero as well - so that example is uninformative. A discriminating example is the set of paths attaining their maximum at a fixed time: it is CapX-polar of the classical Fukushima-Malliavin kind, yet the shift process hits the set of paths whose maximum is attained at time 0 at every record time of B, hence at uncountably many times almost surely. So CapMW of that set is positive while CapX is zero, giving a strict one-way failure. Combined with the trivial implication of E0080 (positive measure implies positive CapMW) this shows CapMW is strictly coarser than Lebesgue-null and not dominated by CapX. The example should be checked against the precise definitions in the source before it is quoted.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The shift generator is a pure translation with no symmetric part in L^2(Wiener), so a non-symmetric Dirichlet form needs a sector condition bounding the shift derivative by the Malliavin derivative - and the shift moves mass off the Cameron-Martin space, so no such bound holds.
method: Write down the generator of the shift and ask what a form for it would have to look like.
obstruction: Without a sector condition the Ma-Rockner theory does not apply and there is no quasi-regular form, hence no capacity calculus. The alternative - a Dirichlet form on the space of stationary increments rather than on Wiener space - changes the state space and loses the pattern sets, which are defined by the path on [0,1].
result: The shift semigroup on C[0, infinity) with Wiener stationary law is generated by the time derivative along the path, i.e. formally by the operator that shifts the path and re-centres it, and this generator is a pure translation - it has no symmetric part in L^2 of the Wiener measure, because the Wiener measure is invariant but the shift is not reversible (reversing time and recentring gives a different process). So a NON-symmetric Dirichlet form in the sense of Ma-Rockner would have to have a sector condition relating its antisymmetric part to a symmetric reference form, and the natural reference form is the OU form. The concrete proposal that follows is: use the OU form as the symmetric part and the shift generator as the antisymmetric part, and the sector condition then becomes a bound on the shift derivative by the Malliavin derivative - which is exactly what fails, since the shift moves mass out of the Cameron-Martin directions. That failure is a prediction that no sector condition holds and that a Dirichlet-form approach must use a different reference form, and it is consistent with E0083's finding that CapMW is not dominated by CapX.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: In d >= 3 hitting times of finite sets have exponential tails; in d = 2 they decay like 1/log t, so the source's three-probability separation collapses and the correct statement is an extremal one for a log-correlated local-time field.
method: Identify what makes d = 2 different, given that the source's higher-dimensional proof is a first- and second-moment computation over hitting times.
obstruction: Proving that form needs the second-moment method for a log-correlated field with the truncated (barrier) argument, which for random-walk local times requires an isomorphism with the Gaussian free field; the isomorphism theorems available (Dynkin, Eisenbaum, Le Jan) hold for the whole field and not for the conditional events in the source's list, where the walk must avoid H for an exponentially long time.
result: In d >= 3 the walk is transient, so the hitting times T_H of a finite set H are integrable with exponential tails determined by the escape probability, and the three probabilities the source lists factor approximately. In d = 2 the walk is recurrent and every hitting time has a heavy (logarithmically corrected) tail: P(T_H > t) decays like c/log t rather than exponentially, so the events in the source's list are not rare on the relevant scale and the moment computation loses its separation. This is the reason the planar case needs the log-correlated structure - the local-time field of the planar walk is log-correlated and the favorite site is an extremum of a log-correlated field, so the correct two-dimensional statement should carry the usual subleading (3/2) log log correction of such extrema rather than being the literal analogue of the higher-dimensional theorems. Predicting the FORM of the answer rather than the proof is the useful output here.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: The planar walk in n steps reaches radius about n^{1/2}, so an annulus at radius n^alpha with alpha < 1/2 sees a local-time field of reduced intensity log(n^{1/2 - alpha}), giving an alpha-dependent extremal constant, while alpha > 1/2 is outside the range altogether.
method: Use the scaling that the source itself supplies: the walk run for n steps reaches distance about n^{1/2}, so an annulus at radius a_n = n^alpha with alpha < 1/2 is well inside the range and one at radius n^{1/2 + eps} is essentially never reached.
obstruction: Turning that into a theorem needs the multi-scale second-moment argument for the local-time field restricted to an annulus, where the field is log-correlated but NOT stationary: the variance depends on the distance to the origin, so the barrier estimates must be run with a drifting barrier, and the standard results assume a flat one.
result: That dichotomy fixes the shape of the answer without any computation. For alpha < 1/2 the annulus lies deep inside the walk's range and the local-time field there is, after time-change, a copy of the field near the origin at a reduced intensity: the number of visits to a site at distance r before time n is of order log(n^{1/2}/r) times an exponential variable, so the maximum over an annulus of radius n^alpha and area n^{2 alpha} should be ((1/2 - alpha) + 2 alpha)^2 times the standard constant, i.e. the extremal constant becomes a function of alpha. For a_n at least n^{1/2 + eps} the walk visits the annulus only o(1) times, so M is zero eventually and the source's conjectured statement degenerates. The interesting range is therefore exactly alpha in (0, 1/2), and the prediction is a one-parameter family of extremal constants interpolating between the origin case and the boundary of the range.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: Dynkin and Eisenbaum isomorphisms are equalities in law, not couplings of level sets; the coupling tool is Lupu's metric-graph isomorphism, which requires the covariance to be the Green function of a Dirichlet form - which the source's modified covariance is not known to be.
method: Ask which isomorphism could give a one-sided inclusion of level sets, since the classical ones are identities in law rather than couplings of level sets.
obstruction: Without an underlying Dirichlet form there is no loop soup, so there is no metric graph and no Lupu coupling; one would have to show directly that E_x[K(tau_n,y)] is a Green function of some Markov process, which requires it to be symmetric and positive definite with the right domination properties, and the source does not establish that.
result: The Dynkin and Eisenbaum isomorphisms identify the local-time field plus an independent squared free field with a shifted squared free field, so they equate LAWS and do not by themselves couple level sets. The tool that does couple them is Lupu's isomorphism, which realises the walk's loop soup and the free field on the same space through the metric graph, and it gives sign information about the field on the cluster structure. So the natural route to the source's inclusion is a metric-graph coupling, and what makes the source's version harder than the standard one is that its covariance E_x[K(tau_n,y)] is the Green function of the walk KILLED AT tau_n rather than at the boundary, so the associated field is not the free field of a Dirichlet form on D(0,n) and the metric-graph construction has no direct analogue. Identifying that as the precise obstacle - the modified covariance is not a Dirichlet Green function - is the useful step.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: p_c tending to 0 makes complete occupation a sparse-nucleation event with small individual influences (the BKS sensitivity signature), while p_c bounded away from 0 makes it majority-like with low-level Fourier weight; the conjecture is that no intermediate behaviour occurs.
method: Test the proposed dichotomy against the mechanism that makes bootstrap percolation sensitive, which is that the final configuration is determined by a sparse set of nucleation centres.
obstruction: The disjoint-union construction changes p_c of the whole sequence to the smaller of the two, so the naive falsification does not immediately work; a real counterexample must keep p_c bounded below while producing high-frequency Fourier weight, which requires a graph whose occupation event is a mixture at a single density.
result: When p_c tends to 0, complete occupation is caused by a small number of critical droplets whose positions are spread over the graph, and each individual bit has tiny influence while the total influence is large - the standard Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm signature of sensitivity, so that half of the dichotomy is structurally right. When lim inf p_c > 0 a positive proportion of vertices are initially occupied and the event is close to a majority-type function, whose Fourier weight sits at low levels, giving insensitivity. The dichotomy therefore matches the two known extremes; what makes it a conjecture rather than a theorem is the intermediate behaviour, and here is a concrete reason to doubt it as stated: the criterion depends only on the numerical value of p_c and not on the graph's geometry, whereas noise sensitivity is a statement about the Fourier spectrum, and one can imagine graph sequences with p_c bounded away from 0 whose occupation event is nevertheless spectrally spread (a disjoint union of a dense part and a sparse part). Constructing such a union is the natural falsification attempt.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
key_identity: One edge of the configuration model can complete a nucleating droplet and change the final occupied set by order n, so the edge-exposure martingale has Lipschitz constant of order n and Azuma-Hoeffding is vacuous here.
method: Check whether the suggested Azuma route can work, by computing the Lipschitz constant of the edge-exposure martingale.
obstruction: Sharp-threshold theorems need a symmetric product measure, and the configuration model's edge set is not a product; transferring requires a switching argument whose error is of the same order as the window being resolved.
result: Switching a single edge in the configuration model can change the final occupied set by an amount that is not bounded: in the supercritical regime a single edge can complete a nucleating droplet whose growth then occupies a constant fraction of the graph, so the vertex-exposure Lipschitz constant is of order n, not O(1), and Azuma gives nothing. This is a genuine obstruction to the source's own suggested route, not merely a technical one, and it is worth recording because the source proposes the route without noting it. The substitute that does work in similar problems is a two-step argument: prove concentration for the SUBcritical quantity (the size of the occupied set below the critical window, which is Lipschitz with constant O(1)) and then use a sharp-threshold theorem (Friedgut-Kalai) to transfer, since the property is symmetric under the automorphisms of the configuration model.

author: claude-prob1000-E-0908
